#6682. The Body and The Teen Drama Fashion Machine

The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable shows to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and new audiences for their sponsors.

Taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has quickly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages. Just this week, the Netflix show has amassed 9.5 million views, marking its second week in the platform’s global top 10. It’s also currently the number one show in 39 countries.

Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.

Fans have responded online, applauding the depth and details of the costuming. “This is why the Y2K clothing in The Body was so accurate,” reads one TikTok with 106,200 views. Another TikTok splices glamorous scenes from the series, showing big sunglasses, velour tracksuits and flip-flops, soundtracked to Gwen Stefani’s 2004 hit, “Rich Girl” (257,000 views).

“With a show set in 2004, the pieces had to feel real — not like a costume of the era,” says Gordon-Crozier, recalling that a lot was sourced vintage and last-minute finds in local Toronto thrift shops. “The ‘J’adore Dior’, the Juicy, the City bag, and the Murakami were the status language of those girls.” Since the show aired, Gordon-Crozier has received hundreds of messages on Instagram asking where pieces are from, along with compliments on the styling. “Y2K fashion was loud, optimistic and completely unembarrassed,” she says. “It was pre-Instagram, so there was no algorithm telling you what to wear.”

True to the period, Gordon-Crozier even recreated tabloid clapback tees, including ‘Team Aniston’ and ‘Team Jolie’ tees for the identical twins Bailey and Britt Bradley. “That generation grew up on new, flashy pop stars like Britney Spears, Paris Hilton and Christina Aguilera, who were all about excess and fun,” she adds. “Today, there’s so much curation. Quiet luxury I’m sure is a response to that in a way.”

“Teen dramas have become Gen Z’s lookbook,” says Rick Jackson, marketing agency Pion’s head of B2B content. “Unlike a traditional ad, a show places a product inside a character, and a lifestyle young people already aspire to.” As such, the City bag or the Juicy Couture tracksuit isn’t just shown, but lived, he explains. “Because Gen Z watches with their phone in hand, an outfit can go from screen to TikTok to checkout within hours,” he adds. This is a big draw for brands, and arguably a far stronger marker of credibility than paid media.

Balenciaga’s City bags were sourced especially for the The Body.

Many brands are wise to this already. H&M consistently ties its collections to Netflix youth hits, channeling the mood of each series into capsules: ’80s retro for Stranger Things, romcom prep for To All the Boys and bold retro looks for Sex Education. This consistency is key. Based on Pion’s recent report into Gen Zalpha (16-24-year-olds), cultural relevance needs ongoing presence in youth culture — on screen, through sport, music and movements — instead of a single, one-off moment.

“Placement gives brands cultural relevance with a generation that’s sceptical of traditional advertising,” says William Weeks, Pion’s chief marketing officer. On the primary market, he explains, interest converts fastest when there’s an accessible entry point. That might mean a discount, a dupe-friendly price point, or a smaller item from the brand. Merch can also fill this gap.

But resale will reap the rewards first, experts agree. Luxury pieces can generate traction as resale offers young fans a way to tap into the moment at a fraction of the price. “For brands, these series are less about a direct ‘buy this exact item’ moment and more about spotting cultural momentum early,” says Sophy Vanner, a strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Often, secondary platforms get the first wave of demand because fans want the hunt and the specific reference point.”

“The smartest brands play both,” says Weeks. “They win the cultural moment on screen and make it affordable for young fans to buy into straight away.”

Vanner argues that another way primary brands can still win is by leaning into the codes, lore and IRL spaces around those moments: “Turning on-screen energy into real-world hangouts, collabs and shared rituals rather than just another product push.”

Euphoria has served as the playbook here, offering everything from pop-ups where guests can have their makeup done, DJ-ed events and talks. In 2022, A24 also launched a makeup line with Euphoria's makeup artist Donni Davy called Half Magic. Globally, the number of TikTok videos posted using #EuphoriaMakeup increased by 1,051% year on year between November 2025 and October 2026, TikTok shares with Vogue Business.

The Half Magic brand was founded by A24 and Euphoria makeup artist Donni Davy.

In February next year, Amazon will air the second season of Benito Skinner’s Overcompensating, a comedy about a closeted ex-footballer. The show has quickly become known for its very 2010s costumes. Already, the first season (aired in 2025) has built a cult following around its preppy fare. Mall prep brands such as J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, and even L.L.Bean have become associated with the male characters.

“We were trying to tap into archetypal ways that people represent themselves — the way that kids try to fit in by overdressing in the version of the thing that they want to be,” says the show’s costume designer Hanna Puley. “For the girls it was a lot of fast fashion. I think we pulled a fair bit from H&M and stuff that was readily accessible and felt familiar. It’s that Forever 21 aesthetic.”

The costuming tracks with a shift that’s been underway for a while among young consumers. Mall brands are having a comeback, accessible luxury is performing (Ralph Lauren revenues climbed 10% in the last quarter), and nostalgic pre-loved designer accessories continue to captivate. It’s exactly why brands should look to these love-triangle, first-kiss dramas to position themselves in the zeitgeist.

Consider also Amazon’s Off Campus, which launched in May and follows a men’s ice hockey team in their heterosexual dalliances. Aside from the usual plot analyses that flood TikTok, the show has also built a strong online contingent of fans wanting to discuss the outfits. Leading female protagonist Allie Hayes, played by Mika Abdalla, appeared in one episode wearing a recreation of Jennifer Lopez’s Donatella Versace-designed dress for Halloween. The piece went viral on TikTok, with creators sharing behind-the-scenes footage of costume designer Charlene Akuamoah at work and, of course, their own reactions. One video shared generated 258,200 views.

“I think part of what makes Off Campus resonate so strongly from a fashion perspective is that the clothing strikes a balance between aspiration and relatability,” says Akuamoah. “I was intentional about mixing contemporary brands, vintage pieces, and different price points to create wardrobes that felt authentic to each character. Younger audiences are increasingly turning to television for fashion inspiration, and social media allows them to immediately identify, share and shop what they see on screen.”

Off Campus star Ella Bright attends the Miu Miu Womenswear Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Across the board, the teen drama genre remains a well for fashion inspiration. Past contenders include US first-love hit, The Summer I Turned Pretty, Spanish private-school thriller Elite and A24’s Euphoria. With them come merch opportunities for the streaming platform and commercial careers for actors beyond the big screen. A24 is no stranger to merch, and after Euphoria, starring actresses Zendaya and Sydney Sweeney have both gone on to become style icons in their own right, closely followed for their press tour wardrobes and brand ambassadorships with Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu, respectively.

“These shows used to be about putting products on screen, but today the real value sits with the cast themselves,” says Alison Bringé, Launchmetrics’s chief marketing officer. She points to the average media impact value (MIV) of an Instagram post from some of The Summer I Turned Pretty’s leading stars: Lola Tung ($387,000), Christopher Briney ($256,000) and Gavin Casalegno ($354,000). “Their fandoms don’t just watch: they follow, recreate and share, which turns these actors into commercial voices with real staying power,” Bringé adds. “That’s why we’re seeing brands sign them as ambassadors rather than treating them as a one-season moment.”

Similarly, Ella Bright, an Off Campus star, commands an MIV of $757,000 per Instagram post. Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty also announced Bright as its first-ever brand ambassador in July. The news culminated in a MIV of $4.6 million within a week and lifted the brand’s overall performance by over 138% the same day, with the top post driving $815,000 in MIV alone. In September, Belmont Cameli, another star from the series, generated $943,000 in MIV in one week for Saint Laurent through a single post.

Devin Barrett, General Idea’s copy director for social and culture, says that teen dramas offer brands a direct link to vibrant cultural conversations and the opportunity to align with future breakout talent. He points to The Body as a fictional portrait of the affluent 2004 teen consumer, explaining that it proffers a new style inspiration source beyond the oversaturated ’00s paparazzi imagery. “Shows like this bring Gen Z and Gen Alpha into an era they didn’t originally experience, orchestrating a richer world around Y2K aesthetics,” he says. “It unlocks the potential for new brand ambassadors with an authentic connection to products like the Dior Saddle bag.”

Of course, fashion has long been a fan of teen dramas, both on television and in the movies. Millennials and Gen-Xers might remember Grease, The Breakfast Club and Mean Girls as historic style inspirations. Shows, however, offer a more enduring marketing avenue for brands to tap into throughout a storyline. “These shows freeze a fleeting, perfect moment — the first love, a friendship group that feels like the whole world,” says Katy Lubin, Lyst’s VP of brand and communications. “The characters are flawed and human. For a brand, being part of that feels genuine in a way a campaign shoot just can’t.” As she sees it, specific pieces become associated with specific character traits, much like the Fendi Baguette gave a cool, New York yuppie association through Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw.

Benito Skinner, director and lead in Overcompensating, attends the Burberry Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Ultimately, because viewers follow shows for long periods across seasons, it means the fashion choices can also shift and evolve, presenting new opportunities for brands. Competitors will need to be agile. Indeed, next season, Overcompensating is leaning into a different vibe, Puley tells Vogue Business. She’s interested to see how viewers react. “We’re not veering so mainstream. There’s a lot more niche stuff,” she says.

#6680. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6677. How Costume Designer Trish Summerville Reimagined ’70s Hollywood Style for ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’

Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is rich in striking, darkly memorable imagery: Margot Robbie shimmying in a sunshine-yellow two-piece at the Playboy Mansion; the sunbaked menace of Brad Pitt’s visit to the Manson ranch; the audaciously bloody denouement, all pit bulls and flamethrowers, playing out high in the Hollywood Hills, with the glittering carpet of nighttime Los Angeles extending endlessly beyond.

But for some—this writer included—the film’s most indelible legacy is its costumes. And, more specifically, those of Pitt’s laid-back (and possibly wife-murdering) stuntman Cliff Booth. Double-denim layers, gold-rimmed aviators, scuffed moccasins—and, of course, those Hawaiian shirts—the character’s late-’60s California cool burnt up the screen and almost certainly played a part in the Americana wave that plenty of menswear fanatics are still riding.

So, when David Fincher stepped into the director’s chair for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth—the Netflix film picks up the story of Pitt’s character nearly a decade later—the task of evolving those indelible looks fell to one of the director’s most trusted creative collaborators: costume designer Trish Summerville. Indeed, the trust ran so deep (the pair had previously worked together on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Gone Girl, and Mank) that Summerville didn’t even know what the project was when she said yes. “I’m always in for whatever he’s doing,” she tells Vogue. “I don’t know anyone else I would do that with.”

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth, Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby, Scott Caan as Charlie Peters, and Carla Gugino as Toni Becka.

Across the eight-year gap between the two films, a lot has changed in Hollywood—not least in its style. By the late ’70s, it’s the heady era of Studio 54 excess, punk-rock rebellion, and Halston halter necks. Still, rather than leaning into disco-fever, polyester-everything clichés, Summerville looked to the real-world period artifacts she could get her hands on locally, scouring the vintage mail-order catalogs and archival racks at Los Angeles’s legendary Western Costume, among other places. Under Fincher’s famously exacting eye, every garment had to serve the story without ever feeling like, well, a costume—and it was a challenge that required building nearly every piece from the ground up. (Though with a little inspiration from some select vintage garments along the way.)

Arguably most seductive of all are the costumes worn by Elizabeth Debicki: in Cliff Booth, the six-foot-three Australian actor plays Karen Crosby, an enigmatic, glamorous Hollywood studio executive whose crisp wardrobe practically gleams within the seedy underbelly of 1970s Los Angeles conjured by the film’s production designer, Donald Graham Burt. Dressed exclusively in varying shades of white—a strict mandate from Fincher that required extensive color-testing with cinematographer Eric Messerschmidt—Debicki’s looks deliberately stand out, but never feel disconnected from the world around her.

“Unless it’s something in the script that really wants the clothing and the costumes to jump off the screen, I never want it to distract,” Summerville says, a sentiment that could apply to the lived-in textures of her costuming work on Cliff Booth as a whole. “It should just help you watch this story.”

Below, Summerville talks figuring out exactly the right cut of 1970s denim for Pitt, looking to Lauren Hutton and Cher as muses for Debicki, and why the decade’s unstudied sex appeal continues to shape fashion today.

Vogue: Obviously, you’ve worked with David a number of times before—but how did this project end up in your lap?

Trish Summerville: It came up through Ceán Chaffin, who’s Dave’s producer. We met at a coffee shop, which was very formal for us, and she didn’t really say what it was—she just said that they had a project coming up, a film, and they’d like me to do it, but she couldn’t tell me what it was because it was quite secretive at that time.

I had to say I was in without knowing what it was. Because of my history with Dave and really liking working with him a lot, I’m always in for whatever he’s doing. I always hope I’m available when he has a project; I hope I’m asked to do it. The only thing I knew was it was a film and it would be in LA, and that was all I knew until I agreed. And then I got an explanation of what it was, and a text from Dave afterwards saying, “Yay, I’m glad you’re in.”

I presume you had seen the first film. Did you revisit it before starting work?

Yeah, I definitely had seen the first film, and after they did call me, I did rewatch it so I could get refamiliarized with the characters, but then I got the script, and realized there’s not a lot of overlap in the characters—it’s pretty much just Brad, so it’s a whole new story about him.

When we last saw Cliff Booth, it was 1969, and this film is set 1977. How did you first start thinking about the ways in which his look—and the look of the city generally—was going to feel distinct from the first film?

I did a lot of research. We have a couple of rental houses here that have pretty extensive research materials, and Western Costume is always a great place to start. They have a search library of periodicals, photographs from sets, behind-the-scenes stuff, and every kind of catalog you could imagine. So it was really important for me to look at everything from films in Hollywood that were happening, behind the scenes, the actors, and then also looking at everyday catalogs like JCPenney or Sears catalogs, looking at Vogue magazine, Ebony magazine—just so I could have a range. It needed to cover what’s depicted on screen as the movie within the movie, then also, how people dressed every day.

Even though there wasn’t fast fashion like there is now, in that amount of time you did see a shift in silhouettes across both men’s and women’s clothing—shapes of jeans, shapes of jackets, the jewelry. But with Brad’s character, it was really about keeping the integrity of who his character is, and the ease—Cliff Booth is really just a fucking cool guy. It was about shifting him a little bit: changing the silhouette of his jeans, giving him Roper suede boots instead of moccasins, not doing as many layers this time, having his shirts buttoned a little bit lower. He’s really, really comfortable with who he is.

Oh, and we definitely wanted to start the film off with the Hawaiian shirt from the first film, so the audience has something to immediately recognize and feel a kinship with.

Tarantino is known for having quite detailed descriptions in his scripts about costumes. Was that the case here?

Yeah, in some instances there were. Some of the descriptions of Cliff, it would say he’s wearing Billy Jack boots, or that he puts on puka shells for when he tends bar. But it wasn’t excessive. We stuck pretty much to anything that was a key story point, or that seemed really integral to the character—he’d maybe describe that he’s wearing sunglasses here, or a leather jacket. With Hot Rod, it would describe the style of clothing he would wear, but nothing as specific as a color or anything like that.

How much of the costumes were sourced, recreated, or made from scratch?

Pretty much most of it was made, at least for our principals. When it’s a period film, and you have stunts, and a really long shoot—we shot, I think it was 105 or 107 days—you really have to have at least doubles of things. It’s too scary. We kind of have a saying in the costume world: “If you have one, you have none.” For Elizabeth, we made her costumes, especially because Dave was very specific that he just wanted her always in a tone of white, and white is very scary in general.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth and Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby.

And with Brad’s character, even the shirts that we found for him—like the Hawaiian shirt and the tiki shirts and the liquor bottle shirt—we bought rayon fabric and printed all those ourselves. For the liquor bottle shirt, one of my shoppers found a vintage one and sent me a picture, and I was like, “Oh my God, that shirt is amazing.” Then I found another one, and then one of the guys in our department said, “Wait, I think I have this shirt at home—I’ve had it for 20 or 30 years.” So we found three different versions of that shirt from the mid-to-late ’40s to the ’70s. I selected all the bottles I liked from the different shirts and changed the colors a bit, and the illustrator I work with drew up a pattern, and then we had a printer here in Los Angeles print up the fabric. We even built jeans for him—we found a Levi’s shape that was great on him, and then we built multiples of them. His barong—the shirt he wears at the end—we ended up making 68 of that particular shirt. It’s all embroidered, all natural fibers, because of how the shirt is used for him and his stunt guy.

Brad knows a lot about fashion—he has his own cashmere line, for one. Was dressing him quite a collaborative process?

It is. He does have opinions, and he’ll bring in inspiration pieces or things that he likes. Then it’s just trying a bunch of shapes, and retrying things once we build them. He really liked the idea of having T-shirts that leaned into an automotive inspiration for Cliff, which makes sense, and we chose to use that at the speedway in the figure-eight races. Working with the Evel Knievel logo, because Evel Knievel was so big at that time, and being a stuntman, he would really have an affinity for that. And then Brad was like, “Oh, I want a red, white, and blue helmet.” So we went to the props guy and said, “We’re going to have this Evel Knievel vibe for him for the T-shirts—could you have a helmet painted for him?”

Brad’s great about little details, like keeping on these native beaded bracelets that he wears always, which wears them in and gives them a lot of life. And he took some of the jeans and his bracelets home at the end, which is nice.

Tell me about working with Elizabeth. Was there anyone specific from Hollywood history or otherwise that you were looking to when figuring out her wardrobe?

I was really inspired a lot by Lauren Hutton for Crosby, because you can’t deny that if you saw Crosby, she could be a fashion model. Even though her character is rooted in reality, she’s very glamorous. Lauren Hutton had this really classic look to her, but very sexy, and with this edge—she would wear very drapey tops and really fitted high-waisted pants with silk blouses. There was also a little Cher vibe too, with the drapey halters. And Elizabeth was a lot of fun to dress. She’s really great about exploring character—with her, it was more talking about who Crosby is and what her day-to-day is like. I always try to work very closely with the production designer and the director of photography. Debicki’s going to be wearing white: how white can I be? Can it be optic white? Does it have to be a toned-down white? For some of her costumes, we had to do two different versions for when she was outside versus inside, because the tones read so differently.

Like Brad, Elizabeth looks amazing in those high-waisted trousers and flares.

She really does. It was so fun. In that figure-eight racing scene when she’s walking through between the bleachers up that little alleyway, it was quite nice to see other people in the cinema take a gasp—because she stands out so much there in this all-white look, so elegant and beautiful. And right before that, when she’s walking down the street at the premiere—so elegant and chic and regal.

Were there any other moments that, when you saw the film on the big screen, you were especially satisfied with?

It’s hard to choose, because I really loved the Manila stills that you see as flash-cut stills—that was several days of shooting, having this whole Filipino vibe, and these brothels, and a Filipino rock band to dress with big platforms and crazy makeup. I also love the scene when Hot Rod is leaving the movie set, and he’s in the velour one-piece Bordeaux jumper with the saddlebags, walking out and talking to Scott Caan. And seeing the tennis scenes—for us, the tennis section was such a big thing because we had to make so many multiples, again all in white, with body-makeup tanner getting on the clothing. And the Verdusco brothers! They would always come together to do their fittings—they never showed up solo—and after we took individual photos, they would always do a back-to-back pose or a karate pose.

As someone who immersed themself so deeply in ’70s fashion for this—an era that’s been cropping up all over the runways recently—what do you think it is about that decade’s aesthetic that remains so aspirational today?

I think it just was cool. People were very sexy without trying to be sexy. You didn’t have to have all your skin exposed—it was something about the silhouette and the drape of the fabrics and the ease. Silk blouses that are just a little bit open, thin gold chains, and the nice drape of the pants. People were so much more carefree then; music was big and fun, and you were out and dancing. I keep joking, “Oh my God, can we please just have jeans with no stretch in them?” Because it’s such a better fit, and the weight of that denim was really nice. Plus you had disco, punk rock, rock and roll: it lent itself to individuality.

Did any of that rub off on your own wardrobe after wrapping the film?

Yeah, actually! For the premiere, I wore the jeans worn by Lauren Glazier, who plays Raquel, Brad’s bartending partner. At the speedway, she’s wearing a pair of ’70s Levi’s with a good boot-cut flare to them, and I borrowed those and wore them to the premiere with a Tom Ford dinner jacket. I definitely had to wear six-and-a-half-inch heels to accommodate the length, because she’s quite tall and I’m not!

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6667. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

The best body trimmers for men are one of the most important grooming tools in your medicine cabinet. And, because dealing with body hair doesn’t always mean shaving it all off, the best body trimmer for you is the one that gives you the results you want.

You might want a multi-purpose manscaper for hitting all points north, south, east, and chest. You might want a skin-so-smooth shaver that leaves you more hydrodynamic than an Olympic swimmer. You might need something that’s body-part specific. ("Best trimmer for balls" is a perennially popular search for a reason.) The point is: No two men will take the same path on their body hair journey. The Philips 7000 is a convincing way to clear some space in the bathroom cabinet. Its bundle pairs body combs for 3mm and 5mm trims with attachments for beard, nose, and ear hair. That gives it a broader role than a dedicated body shaver, particularly if you want to keep some length on your chest.

My usual Philips complaint applies – it still needs its own charging cable rather than the same USB-C charger that works with your iPhone. Long-term testing notes: During three weeks with the 7000, it worked through my thick chest hair without pulling. Its slightly boxy handle was surprisingly comfortable around my underarms, with a textured grip that stayed secure at awkward angles. I also liked how well it handled facial hair, giving me a reason to keep one tool handy for several jobs. Esat Dedezade

While you might be able to get away with leaving your trimmer at home for a weekend by the shore, things have a way of unraveling fast over longer trips and vacations. For extended stays, you’ll want to pack a handy grooming companion to keep you tuned up from head to toe. The Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra is designed to cross state lines and beyond: from the handy travel lock to keep the trimmer from powering on in your carry-on to the high-quality travel case to keep its attachments and charging cable organized.

The unique design of two adjustable length trimming guards allows each to be used to achieve three different lengths, which makes for easy transitioning and also saves space in the carry case. In our testing, the trimmer performed with reassuring power and accuracy. While 60 minutes is not the longest battery life, the trimmer’s constant RPM motor ensures the blade won’t slow down as battery levels dip. In any case, when it is time to charge, the Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra supports USB-C and wireless charging. Adam Hurly

If you’re ballin’ on a budget, Remington’s All-in-One Groomer is a capable, familiar trimmer that shouldn’t set off any fraud alerts on your credit card. Out of the box, this lightweight grooming tool is comfortable to hold, and the blade head twists into place with a satisfying click. The trimmer’s three fixed guards offer a standard spread of lengths, ranging from 3–9mm; and, for anything in between or beyond, the adjustable comb guard unlocks 10 additional length settings between 2–20mm. We were particularly impressed by the adjustable guard, which proved to be a handy tool for safely fine-tuning short to medium-length body hair with confidence. With additional attachments including a nose and ear trimmer, as well as a refined detail trimmer, the All-in-One Groomer lives up to its name, providing full-body coverage at an affordable price. Adam Hurly

Won't settle for anything but the kind of hairless finish worthy of an Olympic swimmer? Philips' Body Groomer 5000 is the device pick up over a conventional trimmer. Its Triple Protect shaving system combines trimming and foil shaving, and there's also a separate trimmer head with adjustable combs covering 1–7mm. So you can leave some length on your chest or switch to the foil for a closer finish.

That head and comb arrangement differs from the British kit I reviewed, which had fixed guards and you’ll also need Philips’ own charging cable. It’s a familiar gripe when rival devices offer charging over UBS-C, but a small one next to how comfortably the shaving system worked for me.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks with the 5000, I used the cutters on either side of the foil to take down longer chest hair, then angled the foil against my skin to clear the stubble. Rushing through dense patches caused the occasional tug, but slowing down solved it. The OneBlade arrived on the scene years back as a hybrid between an electric trimmer/shaver and a manual razor, with replaceable cartridges ensuring you always had the sharpest cutting surface. The Intimate SkinProtect version steps up the game with coated teeth that protect against bites without compromising on stubble maintenance. For truly sensitive areas, I’d still recommend using the low-profile buffer guard to prevent friction or snips. Right out of the box, the Black Ops inspires confidence with its well-weighted, stainless-steel build—wrapped in a grippy rubber handle to eliminate any chance of a slip. While it may sound like something you’d download for your PS5, the Manscaper Black Ops isn’t playing any games when it comes to getting the job done. The trimmer arrives with eight guards ranging from 1.5–13 millimeters, as well as an adjustable guide comb to give you more options for your hair down there. And, like its amphibious namesake, the Manscaper Black Ops is fully waterproof.

We look for trimmers that can get through thick growth without pulling and are easy to control when we get to the awkward bits. We pay attention to how securely the guards fit, how comfortably the handle turns around the body, and how much work it takes to get a smooth finish. Cleaning, battery life, and charging matter, too, especially with a tool that may cover several grooming jobs.

Adam Hurly and Dean Stattmann bring their grooming reviews and health and wellness coverage to this guide, For this update, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his body-groomer testing for British GQ. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation, and advice from celebrity groomer Dan Perri helps explain what to look for and how to maintain the tools.

For a professional opinion on what to prioritize when buying an electric shaver or grooming kit, we sought out the expertise of celebrity groomer Dan Perri, who keeps A-list clients like Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser looking tidy. Here are the key attributes of a good body hair trimmer, says Perri:

“If you want the best performance out of your trimmer, keeping the blade clean and lubricated is key,” says Perri. “Oiling the trimmer every few weeks will keep the blade running smooth, prevent any pulling of the hair, and keep the blade temperature down.” He adds that most trimmers come with a small supply of mineral oil—use it. (Wahl sells a great 4-oz clipper oil for cheap, too.) Be sure to use a machine-safe disinfectant spray to help keep the blade sanitized, which will prevent breakouts, Perri adds.

Can you use a beard trimmer for manscaping?

Some beard trimmers are designed for use on the body, but only if they have attachments designed to keep skin from being pulled into the blade. Keep in mind that the ergonomics of a great beard trimmer doesn’t necessarily align with the ergonomics you’ll want for shaving body parts. You’ll have a harder time hitting hard to reach places, like the back. And beyond that, you’ll want to aggressively sanitize any trimming heads and guards that touch both your face and your… [looks down].

What is the best body hair trimmer for men?

We recommend the Philips Norelco All-in-One 7000 Series for most people who want to keep some length on their body hair. The 3mm and 5mm body combs let you choose how much to leave. For a smooth finish, go with the Body Groomer 5000 Series and its dedicated foil head.

Depends! If you want to be as smooth as an Olympic swimmer, you might want to shave every day. If that's too much of a hassle, doing it every two or three days can be sufficient to have you smooth without your stubble scratching up your shirts.

Do you find body hair unsightly? Then maybe you want to shave your body hair to give yourself a smoother appearance. The decision to trim body hair usually depends on what you or even your partner prefers. For professional sports, a hairless body might be preferred for an advantage, like for swimmers or wrestlers.

Is it better to trim body hair when it's wet or dry?

You can shave your hair whether it's wet or dry, but we prefer doing it on dry hair. Trimmers are able to more easily cut through the hair when it's dry, and you can get more even cuts if you're not going for a clean shave. (Though wet/dry trimmers are all over the market.)

Besides using non-skinsafe grooming electricals (we got you covered in that department), some common manscaping mishaps are the result of poor technique (shaving against the grain), not trimming on cleansed, exfoliated skin, and neglecting post-shaving moisturizing—especially if you have sensitive skin.

Razor burn is no joke. Preparing the skin, using proper shaving technique, and including lotions, moisturizers, and other skin car products into you grooming routine are all good ways to prevent razor burn.

Dan Perri is a celebrity groomer based between NYC, LA, and Florida. His A-list clients include Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser.

#6663. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6660. Elizabeth Debicki Is the Heart and Soul of 'Cliff Booth'

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

It might seem strange, the notion that people have been surprised to find that a David Fincher film, written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt, is “actually good.” But moviegoers had their fair share of reasons to be skeptical of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: chief among them, that Tarantino was forcing a mind-melding of the auteurs that could prove disastrously incongruous simply because he didn’t want to blow his long-awaited 10th and final film on a sequel. The 10-film rule is, of course, completely self-imposed, a mandate Tarantino is stubbornly sticking to instead of realizing he can still employ strict curation and quality control without limiting his filmography to a perfect even number. But now that he’s actually, finally, on what will be his last movie (according to his rules), there’s this notion that he’s afraid to pull the trigger—which some believe he all but confirmed when, in 2023, he announced his 10th film would be called The Movie Critic, only to completely retract that a month later.

Two years later, Tarantino sat down as a guest on (what else?) The Church of Tarantino podcast, hosted by two QT superfans, which is actually a pretty fun listen in between all the excessive stanning. So quickly do they bring up QT10 that it’s obvious the director was anxious to set the record straight. Tarantino tells the hosts that TMC started as an exercise in attempting to write a compelling story about “the most boring” profession imaginable. Despite succeeding, he realized he wasn’t excited by it once the film entered pre-production. There was also a version of the story that he adapted into an eight-hour miniseries, until he realized he had no interest in the process of selling and making TV either.

It’s similar to the way he’s talked about what became Cliff Booth, which started as a novel before morphing into an unwieldy feature script until Pitt convinced him to let someone else take a crack at directing it, lest these titular misadventures go to waste. Watching the film last week, my ears perked up when, in the midst of being courted by Cliff, high-powered Hollywood agent Karen Crosby reveals she got her start in the industry as a… movie critic. She reflects back on her time writing about film derisively, describing the profession as one with a low barrier for entry.

Karen is instantly one of the most beguiling characters in a movie filled with colorful performances both big and small. Played by Elizabeth Debicki with an icy, over-it resolve, Karen’s nagging fascination with Cliff makes for what one critic aptly described as Tarantino’s best-written romance since Jackie Brown. Despite being the closest thing to a co-lead, you walk away from the film feeling like you haven’t seen nearly enough of her.

Later in the film, Debicki gets a showy, highlight reel-worthy monologue where Karen, instead of extolling the virtues of cinema as a former critic might, recites what’s apparently an infamous credo among her close friends: that film, while entertaining, hardly rises to the level of being true art. (This is much to the delight of one of her clients, A-list TV star Charlie Peters, played by Scott Caan.)

It was at this point that I was certain we were watching remixed and repurposed scenes from The Movie Critic—and that if Karen Crosby wasn’t the eponymous character, she was at the very least a gender-flipped version. In one of the only times Tarantino talked openly about his erstwhile film, he said it would be “based on a guy who really lived but was never really famous, and he used to write movie reviews for a porno rag.” Meanwhile, the internet ran with the idea that the film would actually be a not-so-thinly-veiled tribute to Pauline Kael. Karen, for what it’s worth, name-drops Kael when describing her past life.

That this is among the best scenes in the otherwise thoroughly enjoyable Further Mis-Adventures only underscores how silly Tarantino’s 10-film imposition is. Look, l I agree with him: as a logline, it hardly sounds exciting enough to be a career finale, but a Tarantino-directed version of the movie probably would’ve been a good time given how much the director clearly enjoys luxuriating in this world. He can write odes to ‘60s and ‘70s cinema in his sleep. But because it would be a retread with no 11th script to follow, it’ll never see the light of day.

Or will it? I hate to enable weird science, but The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth doesn’t simply work; it’s one of the best movies of the year. Can another director submit himself to Tarantino’s tone and vision the way Fincher does so gamely here? Would Fincher even want to do that again? Hard to say on both fronts, but if Tarantino is going to keep being precious about his next (last?) directorial outing, the least he could do is let someone else execute his other ideas before they start collecting dust. Even Tarantino’s B-Tier is still a great time at the movies.

#6659. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6657. Vintage Watch Experts Break Down Their 6 Favorite Timepieces

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

And another thing, a watch collector might say as they try to sell you on the virtues of the hobby, is that you can bring them anywhere. Unlike other high-value collectibles—cars or paintings, say—you can wear even the rarest of grail-worthy timepieces to, say, a dimly lit bar. Which is precisely where James Fisk—the photographer behind the images in the just-released Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide, written by the renowned dealers Eric Wind and Charlie Dunne—encountered one of the most historic tickers in the book.

Last September, Fisk was at the Waldorf Astoria in New York when he spotted a collector wearing the coveted 1940s Longines model known as the “Tre Tacche.” Watches are challenging subjects even in a photo studio, but Fisk was forced to stumble around the hotel bar looking for any slice of decent lighting to capture the Longines before it slipped through his fingers forever. Used to working on the fly, the photographer keeps 40 or so fabric swatches with him at all times, just in case he needs to lay a watch on top of one as a backdrop for an impromptu shoot.

“You meet someone who just happens to be wearing something really special on the wrist that day, and you have to just be ready for it,” Fisk tells me. It’s how many of the legendary vintage watches—mildly important subjects for a book on the topic—ended up in Wind and Dunne’s new tome.

The book is a comprehensive deep dive into the booming world of vintage watch collecting. Wind and Dunne take readers on a Jungle Cruise-style tour of this sometimes daunting hobby: On your left are the questions that all newcomers should know to ask before buying a vintage watch; on your right, you’ll find testimonies from famous collectors like David Chang, Ronny Chieng, and Daniel Dae Kim; straight ahead are dispatches on the most important brands, from Rolex to Piaget.

Vintage Watches: The Modern Guide is designed to be as welcoming and accessible as possible. While many watch volumes sell for hundreds of dollars, Dunne and Wind made it a point to price theirs at $60 (or $50 on Amazon right now). “A lot of people will be able to afford this book,” Dunne says. “And then, hopefully, they’ll aspire to get some of the watches in it and it’ll ignite their interest in the hobby.”

Below are Wind and Dunne’s favorite selections from the book, including one that the latter was most insistent on including to represent the more affordable side of the spectrum.

There may be two six-figure watches on the cover, but flip just a few pages into the book and you’ll find this delightful little example from Fortis. “I forced Eric to put that in,” Dunne jokes. “He said, ‘We're not putting that in—it's too cheap!” The watch sells for just a touch over $1,000, and this exact piece was in Wind’s collection for several years. He calls it a personal favorite from his years of collecting.

The Shipman might not be historically important or carry great provenance, but it serves an important dimension in the book as a representative for the many types of pieces that comprise a true collection. “Not only [does it show] the range of what is out there as far as exceptional watches at all price points, but also it's one of the most fun and quirky watches in the book,” Dunne says. “You want to have very, very serious watches in your collection, but you also want to have things that put a smile on your face at any price point.”

How do you choose the cover stars for a book about vintage watches? You start with the obvious: The Rolex “Paul Newman” Daytona (bottom) is the poster boy for vintage collecting. The famed Phillips auctioneer Aurel Bacs, who sold the actor’s personal version for a record $17.8 million, calls Newman wearing this special variant “the Adam and Eve moment in Rolex collecting.”

But the Daytona’s partner on the cover, the Audemars Piguet ref. 5516, is an unexpected choice that packs just as much historical heft. “This is one of the most important watches ever made, because of the leap year indicator” Wind says. “AP beat Patek by over 20 years to have a leap year indicator on the bottom. This and the Royal Oak are probably two of the greatest impacts on the Swiss watch industry.” Only nine were made, and Wind sold this example for $545,000 while he was at Christie’s in 2015. I love the specificity of the watch’s leap-year function, which only comes into play once every four years.

Wind and Dunne are longtime evangelists for the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch in the late ’40s and early ’50s. This particular reference is modified to include a tide indicator at the 9 o’clock subdial, done up in extremely pretty tones of sandy tan and deep sea blue. The example featured in the book remains pristine—with a perfect eggshell-white dial—thanks to the original owner stuffing it in a drawer unworn for decades. The watch got to Wind by way of a friend, whom he sent to fetch it from a diner in the original owner’s home state of Arizona.

The watch that Fisk scrambled to shoot in a hotel bar was well worth the hustle. “Longines, in some sense, was Rolex before Rolex,” Wind says. The brand was “the tool watch manufacturer in the 1930s and 1940s, particularly with their Tre Tacche cases. Many of the great aviators and pioneers of the time wore Longines watches.” The model gets its nickname from the three notches on the caseback that helped watchmakers screw the case together tighter to prevent water and dust from getting inside.

This is a classic watch—a defining example of a dress model—done up with a particularly sleek dial. Patek Philippe made endless examples of the 96, allowing collectors to select their favorite flavor from the lot. Wind and Dunne sold this example but both wish they could have it back. “ I don't think it's coming to the light ever,” Dunne laments.

To capture the glossy black dial in the book, Fisk shot the watch at two different angles to mimic the experience of tilting it back and forth in your hands.

The very last watch added to the book was this version of the GMT-Master, one of the Crown’s most important models. The ref. 1675 isn’t the first GMT-Master that Rolex made, but it’s considered the platonic ideal visually and the most collectible among vintage watch lovers. Its predecessors featured troublesome bezels that were prone to cracking, as well as poisonous amounts of radium.

The 1675 was produced for just over 20 years, from 1959 to 1980. This one belongs to Fisk and was on his wrist when we met last week. “We got this right as the pages were printed,” Dunne says, “and we started yelling in emails [to the publisher] saying, ‘We have to stop everything. Put this page in there.’”

#6656. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.
