#6654. Every David Fincher Killer, Definitively Ranked

David Fincher is a rare breed of chameleonic auteur. In the past 40 years, he's directed music videos, commercials, feature films, and television series, all of which keep garnering more cultural importance, either immediately or in retrospect (hey, look, David Fincher directed a 1987 video for a single from a random Philly bar rock band!) Fincher is known for his technical prowess, his “impossible eye,” and his pioneering mastery of digital technology. He’s made love letters to old Hollywood, ripped-from-the-headlines tech-industry autopsies that render depositions as white-knuckle suspense, and popcorn home-invasion flicks. He’s taken turns at IP-franchise stewardship, adapted bestselling airport paperbacks, and told the oddly touching story of a mild-mannered, even-tempered gentleman from New Orleans who ages backwards. But if Fincher has a career throughline, a raison d’etre, it’s his pursuit and depiction of killers—a focus made quite overt in The Killer, a fascinating and highly meta film which hits Netflix Friday after a limited theatrical run over the past two weeks.

In Fincher's films, killers—particularly serial killers—provide an extreme window into human nature. They are symptoms of a sick society, prophets, self-appointed Gods and monsters, blank canvases for us to project our conspiracies and insecurities onto, or would-be celebrities killing for attention from a sensation-hungry media that's all too happy to give it to them. In the pale light of day or the fluorescent light of a prison visiting area, they're often sad, awkward misfits who understand themselves and their actions even less than we do. But by necessity, they're also methodical people who must put a great deal of thought and care into their grisly work in order to continue working. In this way, Fincher sees them as the equivalent of process-mad directors, blocking their victims and staging their crime scenes before selling them to a confused but riveted public.

Time and time again, across his filmography, the image most associated with Fincher is the killer— or the hapless detectives pursuing them—shot from below, almost swallowed whole by a monochromatic backdrop that looms both far above and far behind them, dimly but immaculately lit, and bathed in shadow, inside Fincher's uncommonly steady, all-seeing and all-knowing frame. The killer’s maniacal focus, their certitude, is ours. The detective’s confusion—their understanding that they’re a step behind and a beat late, that they will never get the satisfying answers, the closure they’re looking for—is ours, too.

So for art, and for fun, let’s evaluate the many killers who've made Fincher's body of work as incredible and indelible as it is, based on a shifting, subjective equation of quality, efficacy, body count, and how they’re represented by the auteur himself.

Fight Club is a satire about bereft ineffectual masculinity, about neutered men crushed under Ikea catalogs, about eighth-grade-boy-level rebellion against materialism, capitalism, and every societal convention that places value on anything except chiseled abs, skinned knuckles, bullshit patter, and rugged individualism.

The “kill” here is committed by Edward Norton, as a character identified in the credits as “The Narrator” who murders Tyler Durden—his child, his liberator, his tormentor, and his imaginary friend—by, uh, shooting the side of his mouth, sort of? Somehow, the famously meticulous Fincher lands on a resolution that makes absolutely no sense according to the laws of physical interaction between The Narrator and Tyler Durden established within the rest of the film. Why does this apparition, who knows everything the narrator knows, and can punch The Narrator, can harm him physically without receiving the impact of those assaults, and can’t even be hit by The Narrator, die with his brains blown out as a result of his alter ego shooting off a chunk of his jaw? This is, hands down, the worst “kill” in the Fincher filmography.

22. The Random Guy Who Kills Madonna, “Bad Girl” (1993)

Fincher did his most important music video work for his muse and rumored paramour Madonna, who tapped him to direct videos for hits like “Vogue” and “Express Yourself.” But one of their less heralded collaborations was this bizarre minor work, a video (for a song from Erotica) that plays like a dumbed-down Wings of Desire. Madonna is a stressed-out high-achieving corporate type who unwinds by making bad and eventually fatal decisions. After her Bruno Ganz-like guardian angel (Christopher Walken) makes out with her, she pursues sex with a hookup who clearly intends to murder her. We only see the killer from Madonna's POV, and when he kills her it's presented as her choice, rather than the result of any kind of premeditated plot by the killer; he's more of a prop than a person.

21. Weyland-Yutani Employee, Alien3 (1992)

For a filmmaker who so regularly trades in death, Fincher has depicted shockingly few frivolous ones. Nearly every kill in his work is personal and meaningful. But this is an exception. Towards the end of Alien3 , a commando representing the wantonly evil corporation smokes Francis Aaron, one of the COs on the prison planet Ripley has crash-landed on. The scene underscores the cynical ruthlessness of the outfit, but ultimately it’s just a faceless grunt shooting a stranger.

20. The Security Guard, Fight Club (1999)

In the act of executing Operation Latte Thunder, an ingenious plan to weaponize a piece of corporate art mounted in an office park fountain to destroy a franchise coffee shop in the lobby of a nearby building, Robert Paulson (Meatloaf) is murdered by an extremely extra security guard, who shoots him in the head as he flees the scene of the crime. It’s another somewhat frivolous murder, but the fallout tells us a lot about Tyler Durden’s cult of personality and its effect on its dumbass followers.

19. Frank Underwood, House of Cards (2013-2018)

There are several killers from this groundbreaking, trashy Netflix politico soap you won’t see on this list. This is because the totality of Fincher’s involvement is unclear—he may have imprinted his filmic language on the entirety of the show's run, but he only directed the first two episodes (unlike Mindhunter, his second effort with Netflix, on which he directed seven of 19 episodes across two seasons.) But in the House of Cards pilot, in order to show us just what kind of devious, deliciously shitty archvillain Kevin Spacey's Francis Underwood is going to be, he gleefully, flagrantly bucks the old screenwriting maxim “Don't kill the dog”—and not for the first time—by having Frank strangle his pooch, which has been hit by a car.

The heroine of Aerosmith’s outlier conscious anthem reclaims her narrative by killing her rapist father. It’s an odd “message” song and an odd video, but both were groundbreaking and transgressive at the time. It’s a completely justified revenge killing that Fincher had to sell through suggestion to get played on MTV.

17. Lisbeth Salander, The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Lisbeth (Rooney Mara) slaps the shit out of Martin Vanger (Stellan Skarsgård) with a long iron, then chases him down on her motorcycle as he attempts to flee in a Range Rover, causing him to crash and burn. When she cocks a gun and asks Daniel Craig’s Mikael Blomkvist, “May I kill him?” before lighting out after Vanger, devoid of emotion, it’s the most badass moment of a very badass film.

Bald Sigourney Weaver kills the “Runner” xenomorph by setting off sprinklers after it jumps out of a river of molten lead, causing it to explode. Then—rather than allowing The Corporation to take a parasite chestburster out of her and potentially spare her life—she swan-dives backwards into the lead, killing herself and taking the alien with her—a sci-fi Joan of Arc.

15. Gottfried and Martin Vanger, The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo (2011)

Playing the role of a sicko pervert hiding in plain sight is a stretch for Skarsgård; Martin Vanger is a second-generation killer who shits on his dad for putting up rookie numbers and has a whole secret sex dungeon in his basement where he’s presumably killed dozens of women. Sadly, we must deduct points because Martin ends up dying as a result of overlong monologuing, like a 70s Bond villain.

14. (Tie) Monte Rissell, Rose Barnwright/Frank Janderman/Benjamin Barnwright, Jerry Brudos, Dennis Rader, Richard Speck, Darrell Gene Devier, David Berkowitz, William Pierce Jr., William Henry Hance, Elmer Wayne Henley Jr., Charles “Tex” Watson, Charles Manson*, Paul Bateson, Wayne Bertram Williams, Mindhunter (2017-2019)

David Fincher’s great Netflix series, a history of the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, takes place mainly in the aftermath of its serial-killer subjects' various sprees, so we see few dead bodies onscreen. But as it turns out, talking to killers in quiet rooms and delving into their psyches is just as sensational and disturbing as the graphically depicted comic-book corpses in Se7en. The show is two Feds tearing the cover off America and discovering a teeming morass of perverts beneath the floorboards, up to their necks in muck. What we discover—in this crucial chapter of what feels like a career-long attempt by Fincher to unmake Se7en and its godlike antagonist—is that a lot of these killers are dull, impulsive, mentally-ill misfits and outcasts.

“To support devices," cheers Herman Mankiewicz, after delivering the first draft of his masterpiece, Citizen Kane. In the biopic written by Fincher’s father, booze is the fuel that allows the screenwriter to write, but kills his career one painful, impolitic-outburst-filled social interaction at a time, before it finally kills him, too. Alcohol is the lubricant that powers Mank’s genius, even as it obfuscates that genius and speeds his demise. The bottle both makes him and unmakes him, like Popeye if spinach destroyed his liver. It’s a self-inflicted slow killer, which makes its work all the more painful and tragic to witness.

12. (Tie) Raoul & Burnham, Panic Room (2002)

In Fincher’s masterful and inventive “conventional” thriller, Raoul (Dwight Yoakam) domes spoiled, insufferable, cornrowed Junior (Jared Leto) when he tries to walk away from the robbery they're pulling. Later, Burnham (Forest Whittaker) sacrifices himself and $22 million in bearer bonds to kill Raoul and save the day. Hard to say which is more satisfying.

11. Tobacco, American Cancer Society Commercial (1985)

The Big Bang of Fincher’s career, when he transitioned from Industrial Light & Magic cameraman and matte photographer to auteur. His first effort was this commercial, made for just $7,000, which several television stations banned because it was too graphic and disturbing. We have to side with the networks on this one—it’s a truly horrifying ad, a nightmare vision of the Starchild puppet from 2001 as a fetus double-fisting darts in the womb. But it’s an impressive work of visceral agitprop, one that had the potential to reconfigure the way we thought about this deadly but fairly common behavior in the 80s.

In Fincher’s latest, Michael Fassbender plays the unnamed, titular assassin in a procedural that’s all process. He's a classic Fincher protagonist, a type-A creature of habit and ritual. The wrinkle is he kind of sucks at his job—or at least, when we meet him, has reached a point where he’s no longer able to execute his work according to the dispassionate code he lives and works by.

So, yes, he’s obviously baited into killing John Doe, and basically gets his wife killed by being an idiot and giving his name to her killer in an angry impulsive rush when John Doe is right next to him pretending to be a nosy reporter, and by giving into his emotions and impulses he’s throwing his life and his career away—but Mills ranks this high because of Pitt's incredible work in the tortured moments before Mills fulfills John Doe's master plan. It's an all-time great performance that's seared into your brain forever after you've watched it once.

8. The Verdusco Brothers, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

Matt Groove and JB Tadena play Eddie and Fernando Verdusco, the gangster antagonists that walked directly out of Quentin Tarantino’s cinema-fried brain and into Fincher’s latest. The film has been sold as a play on a chatty Elmore Leonard crime story, but with touches like the Verduscos, it’s more like a muddy puddle of all different stripes of exploitation film, from noir to horror to splatter. The Verduscos are Filipino but present as Yakuza hitmen, with a dash of Mortal Kombat cartoonishness. It’s easy to give characters badass motherfucker names that insist upon themselves, with writers and directors who simply expect us to find them scary and cool with little to no proof besides a slow-mo entrance and a needle drop. But Tarantino and Fincher earn the mythology with a particularly terrifying and gnarly introductory home invasion murder (invoking Panic Room) of a family of four. Esmeralda, the rhino-killing war hammer brandished by Fernando, has the instant iconographic “weapon as characterization” power of which Tarantino’s longtime friend and collaborator Robert Rodriguez would be envious.

Alien3 is Fincher’s canon event; the formatively traumatic experience of tangling with a cynical studio on his first feature made him the director he became. Having the film taken away from him taught Fincher the importance of demanding complete creative control. So it’s either ironic or brilliant that in many ways, this Xenomorph is a metaphor for the director, an alien antagonist (with the characteristics of a rabid dog!) resisting a sinister corporation that wants to cage and exploit him for its own evil purposes.

6. Time, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008)

In a movie about a guy born as an old man who ages in reverse, a byproduct of his disease is Benjamin (Brad Pitt) must “blend in”, experiencing his childhood in an old folks home where death is routine. Benjamin Button lives outside of time, breaks the rules of time, and in the process explains the ravages of time. Throughout the film we watch everyone around Benjamin die: From war, from old age, from disease, and finally, from being born in reverse. It contains the most stunning and heartbreaking kills in Fincher’s filmography because they are not a product of a sicko's grand design, but simply nature taking its course, harrowing in its obvious, matter of fact inevitability.

The breakout star of Mindhunter, Edmund Kemper was the Co-Ed Killer—a hulking monster who killed many people and occasionally had sex with his victims' decapitated heads—and in the show, he’s the catalyst for the birth of the behavioral science unit. Cameron Britton plays Kemper as a verbose, precise, calmly menacing giant with thick frames and a trim mustache. He’s the most Fincheresque antagonist in the series. Kemper is lucid and clear-eyed, incisive, articulate, and occasionally even funny. Understanding what he’s done—and exactly why and how he did it— is critical to the protagonists' mission, and Kemper understands this, which makes him that much more terrifying.

Another meticulous, disciplined Fincher avatar who has checked every box and arranged for every contingency. Amazing Amy is a feminist archvillain exploiting misogyny to liberate herself from the American prison of marriage and the cool-girl wife’s role therein. She’s a deeply petty scorned woman of iron will, expert at manipulating the public, the authorities, staged crime scenes, and her husband.

3. Cliff Booth, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026)

In their fourth film together, Fincher and Pitt unlock their greatest character, which is doubly impressive when you consider that, the first time we met Booth, it earned Pitt his long-awaited Oscar. This version of Cliff Booth, nearly a decade older and mostly washed, is a more interesting character and one of Fincher’s greatest killers because he unlocks a darkness that is only hinted at in Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood. In that film, Cliff is an affable and doggedly loyal sidekick. When he kills (on screen), it’s self-defense, protecting his buddy from harm, and you can squint and think, “This just might be a roughneck, badass dude with a heart of gold.” In this installment, Cliff operates according to his personal moral compass, which in some cases involves premeditated, entirely avoidable, cold-blooded murder. He’s observing a uniquely American form of zen, existing in an overloaded sensory flow state on a spectrum that encompasses all manner of kinetic pleasure, remaining at ease and even-keeled whether he is bartending, Demolition Derby driving, getting slapped by a Goddess with frying pan hands, running a film projector at the New Bev, clutching an Old Chattanooga, or, of course, killing.

The film, and the killer, that has in many ways defined Fincher. Speaking to Esquire, before releasing Zodiac, the director said, “I don’t want to make a film serial killers masturbate to.” The line was an obvious dig at his own second feature, which is pure serial-killer porn and would set the template countless lesser movies would aspire to going forward. John Doe is a true mastermind who executes creative, horrific, gimmicky murders inspired by the Bible's deadly sins. But most importantly, he’s always a step ahead, always smarter than the cops coming after him, and his win at the end is absolute. Morgan Freeman’s terrified exclamation at the film's climax sums up the plot of the whole film: “John Doe has the upper hand!”

In Fincher’s masterpiece of form and statement, he’s at the height of his powers, revisiting the serial killer as a “celebrated” cultural figure and a malignant expression of society, and what he comes back with is maddening emptiness. Instead of a running inner monologue, we’re given nothing—not even the killer's identity (or identities.) The first half is a painstakingly made and researched film, scrubbed of all romance and sentimentality, that comes as close as fiction can to mimicking the endless, mundane texture of reality. Then, the killer dissolves.

To Fincher, the Zodiac Killer isn't a person, but an idea, an unanswered question, an unresolvable puzzle. Although different actors show up playing people who might be the culprit, the Zodiac haunts the film mostly as an absent menace. Conflicting motivations and theories are thrown at the viewer and it’s impossible to sift what circumstantial evidence is real from bullshit. Some characters favor one suspect, some another, nothing ever adds up, and no one is ever proven conclusively right or wrong. Years pass, people fall in and out of life, they succumb to their demons. Only devastating, lonely obsession remains.

#6653. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested—and retested—just about every meal delivery service. Each time we try HelloFresh, we’re impressed by its bold flavors, so we teamed up with the brand to bring you our favorite recipes each week (read more about how we chose them here). Sign up for a delivery, and you also get a 3-month digital subscription to BA for free. Here’s a closer look at one of our BA Picks.

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

True to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

#6652. Are You Ready for the ’80s Fashion Revival?

Rejoice: shoulder pads and opulence are back.

It happened suddenly: golden shades, huge shoulders, stacks of oversize jewelry. At Anthony Vaccarello’s swan song for Saint Laurent, it was all golden with big jackets, safari suits, and joyfully ruffled blouses fit for a Joan Collins-era Dynasty, but built for 2026. For spring/summer 2027, the ’80s have been a big focus. Valentino showcased jewel-toned gowns with piled-on maximalist pearls, and Giorgio Armani’s strong shoulders were straight out of a fashion history book. Mugler and Calvin Klein did strong silhouettes that alluded to the era. And even Louis Vuitton couldn’t help but look back to New York in the 1980s for its recent cruise collection, presenting models in stiff jeans and Keith Haring tops.

And why not? The ’80s were a time of experimentalism and personality, making it ripe to be mined for fashion inspiration and also less referenced than the forever hall of famer ’90s and Y2K style that fashion can’t stop loving.

The obsession has already started (or, rather, it never really ended) in the vintage world. Haile Lidow, founder of Lidow Archive, has seen a demand recently for her vintage drop waists and ruffle-skirt dresses in wild patterns. “I have so many in my collection that have gone neglected for years and are finally being noticed,” she tells ELLE. “Also, the ’80s power suits! They are back! Sometimes I update the skirt length if it feels too dated. We call it ‘minify’ but regardless, the requests for these are pouring in.”

For some, it’s about nostalgia, but for others, it’s totally new. Violet Sky, a 26-year-old Gen Z singer first became inspired to dress totally ’80s after watching the film Girls Just Want to Have Fun while she was in high school. “It was all the bright colors and just how fun everything was and the big hair,” she tells ELLE. “I just felt really drawn to it. I didn’t really have my own personal style, and so at that moment, I was like, well, why don’t I just explore this?” She started by pulling pieces from her mother and grandmother’s old wardrobe in her attic, and now exclusively wears acid-wash denim, tops bedazzled with rhinestones, and Reebok Classics every day.

“I think fashion, and interiors, and so many other aesthetic-based industries has been stuck in a really boring rut that’s been disguised as minimalism,” adds Lidow. “It started in the late ’90s as ‘chic’ and developed into an excuse for society to try less. The ’80s were the opposite: one bangle was never enough, you had to have four. Eyelids were splashed in bright colors and patterns were clashing all over the place. I think we’ve finally grown bored of the boring. We want to have fun again.”

Even fashion historians can’t help but think of the ’80s as a sort of golden age of fashion, when Vivienne Westwood and Christian Lacroix were sending highly creative pieces down the runway. Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, even associates the era with a shoe renaissance, which we’ve also been experiencing in 2026 with the rise of It shoes. “I think what we’re seeing in part may be a hope that we can come back to a period when fashion really was fashionable, because now we’re seeing so much dissatisfaction with fashion, and with the costs of fashion, not only personally, but also to the environment, and to workers and so on,” she tells ELLE.

The familiar feeling of power dressing in the air (and on the runways) with these ’80s silhouettes is deeply tied to the female gaze. “What you see in the ’80s is that it’s coming out of a feminist movement that was growing in the ’70s, and then in the ’80s became a somewhat different feminist movement, so it was more kind of, girly, economic feminism rather than a sort of leftist, ideological feminism of the ’70s,” adds Steele. “So instead of working-class androgyny, you had suits like men had. You had powerful shoulders, you had a look of Amazonian femininity going down the runway, and that resonated with a kind of booming market, and a period when maybe, maybe feminism was becoming more commodified, or that was certainly a period when people realized that they could market specifically to women by having things that look both powerful and sexy.” Who can argue with that?

“I think that bright colors and loud fashion of the ’80s is something that’s so opposite than what’s kind of like going on today at least in everyone’s everyday life versus the runway,” adds Sky. “People are kind of intrigued about that. And they want to maybe try something different.” The ’80s revival may be nostalgic, but its appeal feels entirely of the moment: it’s instant personality in an era of sameness.

#6649. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman says. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#6647. The Scoop with Kolor’s Taro Horiuchi: On His Zara Collab

Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

This week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago. Before that, Taro was running his namesake womenswear label, which he launched after moving to France in 2010, as well as a menswear line called TH Product, founded in 2018 (the two merged when he took over Kolor in 2025).

Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively. The thread that seems to bind Taro’s work together is turning basic garments on their heads, which is also what he sought to do in his most recent collaboration with a little conglomerate called Zara. I called him up to discuss that and more.

On December 3, we will be launching a collaboration with Zara. We are hosting a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2, and the global launch will be the following day. It’s the first global collaboration we’ve announced since I took over as creative director in 2025, so I feel honored to be in this position. The collection will span womenswear, menswear, and childrenswear. It’s the first time Kolor is making kids’ clothing, so that was an interesting challenge for us.

Shots from the Kolor x Zara campaign. It’s the brand’s first global collaboration since Horiuchi took over as creative director from founder Junichi Abe in 2025.

What was it like designing children’s clothes then?

The core challenge for us in this project was expressing the brand without the high pricing and intricate details. We wanted to make good, interesting clothes regardless of whether it was for children or adults. However, there are constraints when it comes to making clothes for children, both in terms of the textiles you can use and because the accessories and the parts on the clothing are very small. That was definitely a learning experience for us, which we took on happily.

Can you tell me a little bit about the collection? What was the inspiration behind it?

So the theme for this project is “World Uniform”. It’s something we do at Kolor: take something basic and turn it into something a little different. Fans of Kolor are always on the cutting edge of fashion, and they are always seeking something new. But those who shop at Zara are looking for clothes for their daily lives. So our challenge was to find the perfect balance between familiar and inspirational.

Behind the scenes of the Kolor x Zara campaign shoot. The collection’s theme, “World Uniform”, reflects Kolor’s habit of taking basic garments and making them “a little different”.

For sure, there are those who go to Zara for basics, but I’d argue that’s changing because of all the luxury brand collaborations Zara orchestrates, including the one with Kolor.

One thing that really stood out to me through this experience was the very high quality of fabrics and operations that Zara offers. My family and friends wear a lot of Zara, though I personally haven’t, so I wasn’t aware of the way they work. But the whole process was very inspirational to me. Both the product quality and the speed of responding were quite remarkable.

I remember when Zara launched in Greece; I was about 8 or 9. My mother was delighted because she could buy cheap but nice clothes for us. I still have some of those sweaters from 30 years ago, and my son wears them now. Has it been fun to work with Zara’s manufacturing resources?

For sure. When it comes to any collaboration, it doesn’t make sense for me to make anything you can make alone. I am very happy to say we managed to realize something that Kolor couldn’t have made on its own, and I believe Zara feels the same way about us.

A look from Kolor x Zara, which launches globally on December 3 after a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2.

You’ve taken over Kolor from its founder. It feels like a tough gig to follow a founder who is still involved and alive. But if we look at people like Julian Klausner at Dries Van Noten and Haider Ackermann at Tom Ford, maybe that’s part of the success recipe? How do you work with Junichi Abe, and is there a lot of pressure to match him?

I’ll answer your second question about pressure first. Of course, I feel the pressure, and I also respect Abe-san incredibly. Whether it’s a recipe for success, I’m not sure yet. What I can say is that the core value and DNA of a fashion brand aren’t something you can build in one day. It takes time. All I can do is what Abe-san told me to do at the very beginning of my time at Kolor: “Don’t repeat what I could. Just make Kolor unique to you,” he said.

There are quite a few open positions at the big luxury houses at the moment, and we expect them to be filled any day now. Does the constant change-up in creative directors affect the way you and other designers work or view the industry?

Things change much faster than when I started in fashion around maybe 2005. As I was saying earlier, building a brand takes time because it needs to have a culture and a philosophy. The compatibility of the brand and the designer is very important too in all that. In that sense, speedy changes are not good because they don’t allow the two to get to know each other.

Kolor x Zara. Horiuchi says the collaboration let him make something Kolor “couldn’t have made on its own”, thanks to Zara’s fabrics and production speed.

Applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. You won the Diesel Award at ITS 20 years ago. How necessary are those awards and prizes to young designers?

I graduated from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 2007, and I am still so thankful to Barbara (Franchin, founder and director of ITS) and Renzo (Rosso, founder of Diesel and founder and chairman of OTB) for the opportunity. Looking back now, this was a big turning point in my career. It wasn’t so much about winning the award, but more about the people I met. Demna was in the year above me at Antwerp, and together we organized an exhibition about Japan. At the Diesel award, I met Matthieu Blazy, who is now at Chanel. So, for me, those prizes and competitions are meaningful because of the communities they draw together. If you want to tell what the future of the industry will be in 20 years, you should look at who is entering those competitions now.

But I have a concern about the future of the industry. When I was a student, the tuition fees for Antwerp were around €1,000 per year. Now, for non-EEA students, it’s between €13,000 and €25,000. The people who can’t afford such high tuition will not be entering the fashion industry. Demna wouldn’t have been at Antwerp if the tuition was any more expensive. So maybe, one suggestion for the organizations that support those awards would be to focus more on scholarships and grants.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday offer equally good clothing deals. #6645. Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

While the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

When the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

#6643. The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

Finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles. (No piece of sushi has ever needed gold leaf so liberally applied.) Historically, to eat well, you’ve had to splurge: it isn’t cheap, after all, to source top-quality fish in the British capital, and it’s still worth saving your pennies for a blowout meal at one of the city’s top omakase counters, such as Sushi Kanesaka or Sushi Tetsu.

But in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou. (Its former location next to the old Condé Nast offices on Hanover Square led it to be nicknamed the “Vogue canteen.”) And that’s without mentioning beloved neighborhood spots like Uchi Hackney or Jin Kichi in Hampstead.

From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.

Located within the ritzy 45 Park Lane hotel, this Michelin-starred, omakase-only destination with 13 seats is as atmospheric a sushi experience as you’ll find anywhere in London. Step through the discreet noren curtain that marks the entrance, and you’ll feel as if you entered a portal straight to Kyoto, with the gently lit interiors—all hinoki wood, lime plaster walls, and intricate kumiko lattice work—serving as a delicate backdrop for the equally delicate flight of dishes that follows. Helmed by legendary chef Shinji Kanesaka, the 13-seat restaurant offers a masterclass in traditional Edomae-style omakase using an impressive array of locally sourced ingredients: a silky pot of chawanmushi topped with the briny sweetness of fresh Cornish crab; marbled, melt-in-your-mouth fatty tuna nigiri with perfectly seasoned rice sourced from Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture; a Scottish lobster presented on a board then whizzed up into shatteringly crisp morsels of tempura. With a price tag of £420 per person, it isn’t for the faint of heart—but for those seeking true perfection, it’s London’s ultimate bucket-list sushi destination. —Liam Hess

A true Mayfair stalwart, Kiku has been serving the neighborhood since 1978, making it one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city—and unlike some of its flashier neighboring sushi restaurants, Kiku’s vibe is one of calm, quiet elegance. It’s the place to go for a consistently excellent, no-frills sushi experience where the quality of the fish speaks for itself, whether it’s the salmon and tuna in a classic sashimi set, or rare delicacies like Hokkaido sea urchin and sweet prawn served on perfectly seasoned rice. The tempura here is world-class, with a light, lace-like batter, and the £40 lunchtime set menu—which consists of yakitori, tempura, sushi, miso soup, and a dessert—is one of the best deals in central London. The ultimate seal of approval? It’s a favorite spot among the staff at the nearby Japanese Embassy on Piccadilly. —L.H.

This low-key but stylish joint, which opened in 2024 in a bijou shopfront on Brewer Street, is the brainchild of chef Takamasa Mogi—also the founder of popular Mayfair spot Cubé—and serves up astonishingly good sushi to the 10 seats that surround its subdued but stylish hinoki wood counter. (Soho regulars will remember the building’s former life as a manga store and karaoke bar—it turns out there’s still a karaoke room downstairs if your omakase dinner ends up getting a little raucous.) I was especially impressed by the creative but not overdone nigiri, including smoky slivers of seared Korean turbot and Spanish tuna with Oscietra caviar, served atop pillowy beds of red vinegar-seasoned rice. Given the quality, it’s excellent value too: the lunchtime menu offers salad, seven pieces of omakase nigiri, and dessert for £51.80, while the dinner menu of two appetizers, nine pieces of omakase nigiri, a temaki roll, and dessert comes to £89. (They also do a well-priced pre-theater menu if you’re planning to catch a West End show.) —L.H.

Under former Noma sommelier Yuki Kaneko’s ownership, Yuki Bar has transcended East London’s small plates and orange wine scene. Within the low-lit, 20-cover spot soundtracked by disco J-pop, dishes riff on French and Nordic classics with Japanese inflections, like a sesame-studded take on oeufs mayonnaise, embracing home-style cooking and a choose-your-own-adventure menu of “snacks, littles, and larges.” A few portions of house-made potato crisps with sansho pepper and grilled onigiri kick the evening off, while rotating mains have included an aromatic chicken hot pot and blushing strips of beef tataki silken with soy sauce and mustard. Go with a group, be greedy, and get a few bottles recommended by Kaneko. —Anna Cafolla

Mayfair isn’t exactly short on high-end sushi counters, so it takes serious pedigree to make a splashy entrance here. One of the few people capable of that is Shogo Amamoto, the Fukuoka-born chef behind Taipei’s two-Michelin-starred Sushi Amamoto—a reservation so notoriously tough to secure that die-hard sushi-heads are known to plan trips to Taiwan around it. (Sushi mastery clearly runs in the family: his brother, Masamichi, helms Tokyo’s cult-favorite Higashiazabu Amamoto.) Chef Shogo’s London outpost forgoes the usual Mayfair glitz in favor of a serene, minimalist room centered around a pale hinoki wood counter and bespoke Japanese ceramics, and the focus lies firmly in classic Edomae culinary craft. Dishes feature top-tier seafood flown in from Tokyo’s Toyosu Market alongside standout European catches—translucent slices of French wild seabass sashimi with shiso flower and ponzu, a sweet seared Orkney scallop wrapped in crisp nori, or rich, smoky nodoguro whose skin crackles straight off the grill—and warm, perfectly seasoned rice. It’s purist without feeling oppressively solemn—and one of the freshest (in every sense) new additions to London’s luxury sushi roster. —L.H.

One of London’s sexiest counter seats (and that’s saying something), Ushio arrives from Fukuoka, on Japan’s Kyushu island. Its first European location, Ushio serves A5 wagyu omakase style (no sushi here!), specifically akami wagyu that has been imported from Japan. It’s leaner and higher in protein, with a taste that will unfurl across an incisive multi-course menu of wagyu every which way. You’ll get a card that tells you which prime cut of beef you’re eating with every course, and it’s certainly a journey. Some are barely kissed by the grill, others draped in a rich sukiyaki marinade or glazed in their signature tare sauce. A trio of tenderloin, tongue, and kurimi are delicately salted and presented gloriously as is. (My tip? Say yes to the extra curry course! If it wasn’t so sophisticated in there, I would be licking the bowl. Add the sake pairing and enjoy your time with the very charming sommelier too.) Finish with a (meatless, but still mighty) matcha choux puff. In a quiet, darkened corridor of Fitzrovia, the minimal interiors are stunning and sleek, just like the Fukuoka flagship, built around wood and stone with Ko-Imari porcelains and hand-built ceramics by Taeko Kajihara. And everyone who works there just seems cool! A spot that lingers long on the palate. —A.C.

Tucked behind a bright white storefront in Clerkenwell, this seven-person omakase experience is among the city’s toughest reservations to secure. Husband-and-wife duo Harumi and Toru Takahashi are behind the operation (the latter being the chef), both of whom are famously warm and welcoming, fostering a convivial atmosphere versus the buttoned-up formality of traditional omakase settings. The seasonal menu relies on what is strongest in the market that day, but expect sushi so fresh it melts in your mouth and impeccable sake pairings. The restaurant sits along Jerusalem Passage, an 18th-century path to the priory of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, which later transformed into a pedestrian walkway linking St John’s Square to Aylesbury Street. —Nicole Kliest

If you’re craving sushi but aren’t in the mood for a formal omakase environment, Uchi Hackney achieves an exceptional balance. This ultra-cozy spot in a residential area of Hackney leans on traditional Japanese design motifs (linen, ceramics, wood), and even encourages guests to kick off their shoes and slip into a pair of provided slippers. The restaurant began as a delivery service in 2015 and now offers a high-quality menu in its brick-and-mortar location, serving both brunch and dinner. As for the dishes, expect a variety of hot favorites such as grilled pork belly skewers and lightly deep-fried tofu, and savor the selection of fresh sushi and sake to round out the experience. (An aside: Uchi Hackney’s intimate ambience makes for the perfect date night locale.) —N.K.

Set on the ninth-floor Liverpool Street branch of Los Mochis, arriving at Luna Omakase comes with a delightful sense of ceremony. As the evening begins, you’ll be guided with your group from the bar along a nondescript corridor to a set of sliding doors that are opened—with plenty of theatrical flourish—to reveal the 12-seater dining room, where a sculptural timber counter is lit with a lunar glow against a backdrop of glittering skyline views of the City. Over the course of 12 seasonal plates, the vibe is lively and conversational, as the sushi masters hand each pristine slice of aged fish—think melt-in-your-mouth otoro tartare with Oscietra caviar served with a cloud of smoke, or juicy king crab leg nigiri with feathery shavings of yuzu—and artfully balance traditional technique and off-the-cuff flourishes throughout the meal. (If you fancy it, you can also make the evening more spirited—quite literally—courtesy of the tightly curated list of rare sakes and Japanese whiskies that the team is more than happy to geek out over, and that will serve as an instant conversation starter with your fellow sushi obsessives.) It’s intimate and undeniably stylish, but free of the stuffiness that can make your typical high-end omakase experience feel a little intimidating. —L.H.

In operation for nearly 30 years, this beloved sushi institution now operates across eight outposts in London (plus six in Tokyo). For those who favor great value and generous portion sizes, this restaurant chain consistently gets top marks. Choose from a menu of sushi, sashimi, nigiri, chirashi, unagi, or opt for a bento box to get the full experience. Their latest creation worth dining out for? Wagyu with black tobiko (or a ‘sushi taco’, as it’s so nicknamed). —N.K.

This Japanese udon noodle bar opened its doors in Soho back in 2010 and has since expanded to three popular London locations, plus a shop offering provisions such as chilli oil and jars of Fukujinzuke. The original location is worth a visit for the freshly made noodles and dashi alone, but don’t sleep on the weekly blackboard specials either (previous highlights include grilled corn with miso butter and fried whitebait with shibazuke cucumber). Koya Soho is walk-ins only and is open from breakfast through to dinner. —N.K.

This is where you go when you want authentic Japanese food and a killer sake selection, all in a calm, relaxed setting. Chisou’s two central London locations—Mayfair and Knightsbridge—treat guests to seasonally changing dishes and a menu of wow-worthy raw fish, with the option to sit at a sushi bar or at an intimate table. And back to the sake for a moment: Chisou prides itself on having one of the largest menus around, with experts on hand to suggest pairings and special events like sake and British cheese pairing classes led by specialists. —N.K.

A charming, intimate spot tucked away on New Quebec Street in Marylebone, Roketsu recently relaunched as a rare example in London of kappo-style dining, where the chefs will whip up a customized set menu based on a conversation about your preferences at the beginning of the meal. The team of chefs here take a creative approach to classic Japanese cuisine, folding in a handful of French flourishes: most notably, perhaps, with one of the restaurant’s signature dishes, an opening bite of a crisp wafer filled with 10-day miso-marinated foie gras. (Other highlights included Cornish cod with a vibrant nori sauce, and flame-grilled wagyu beef with yuzu oroshi for a clean, citrus-forward finish.) With an open kitchen behind a hinoki wood counter, Roketsu is an elevated, classically Japanese dining experience—but it also comes with an element of choose-your-own-adventure fun that makes it feel genuinely unique. —L.H.

If you’re seeking a quirkier spin on omakase dining, head over to Notting Hill, where you’ll find the six-seat Juno hidden in a speakeasy-like space at the back of Los Mochis, the popular neighborhood Mexican-Japanese restaurant on Uxbridge St. The dining room’s delightfully funky, “Tokyo-meets-Tulum” decor—bamboo, seagrass, high-gloss wallpaper—should serve as an initial clue for what to expect here: the textures and flavors of Japanese cuisine are lent a fresh twist courtesy of a bold, Mexican-inspired toolkit of spices, acids, and smoke. (Think chutoro spiked with a sharp kick of fermented jalapeño, or red bream brushed with lime aioli and topped with a sprinkle of crushed-up Oaxacan flying ant for a surprisingly delicious note of nutty earthiness.) Bring your friends and make it a party. —L.H.

There are few more scenic spots for lunchtime sushi in London than chef Endo Kazutoshi’s rooftop restaurant, which sits proudly above the Raffles London hotel at the Old War Office—and trades the monastic restraint of Endo’s Michelin-starred White City flagship for sweeping views over Horse Guards Parade. Grab an outdoor table and browse a menu that bridges Japanese precision with Mediterranean flourishes, the latter a direct nod to the years Kazutoshi spent cooking in Spain. Most of the dishes are built for sharing, so order generously: try the tuna tartare on miso brioche, the yellowfin tuna “chorizo” (its smoky, paprika-laced punch is balanced by pickled tsukemono and warm pita), or the charred, melt-in-the-mouth octopus with miso, fava beans, and asakura sansho—it’s all rather decadent, but somehow never overly heavy. Come for the pristine, perfectly seasoned nigiri; stay for the golden-hour sunset over the Neoclassical rooftops of this stately corner of central London. —L.H.

Many of the best Japanese restaurants fall into two categories: no-frills neighborhood ramen and udon spots, or the kind of hushed, six-seater omakase counters where you might be frowned at for asking for extra soy sauce. Aki London, tucked inside a soaring, Grade II-listed former bank on Cavendish Square, couldn’t be more different. Designed by Francis Sultana, the dining room is all about pure, flamboyant glamour—think fluted marble columns, soaring coffered ceilings, and plush velvet banquette seating. This isn’t a case of style over substance, however: The kitchen leans into farm-to-table Japanese cooking rooted in Kyoto traditions, ranging from crisp, featherlight tempura rock shrimp to delicate steamed-and-crisped wagyu gyoza, to smoky, tare-brushed chicken thigh skewers straight off the robata grill. Whether you’re coming for a leisurely lunch or a late-night dinner, make sure to check out the subterranean cocktail bar first for a round of yuzu-infused martinis. (Aki is best enjoyed in the company of a lively group.) —L.H.

A neighborhood restaurant in the truest sense, Jin Kichi’s cult following makes booking a table a competitive sport. This tiny, two-floor restaurant is cozy, often crowded, and wonderfully authentic. While the yakitori is a major draw, the sushi and sashimi are of a quality that rivals the city’s most expensive counters. It’s the kind of place where the chefs know the regulars by name (and where said regulars might be the likes of Kate Moss and Harry Styles). —L.H.

#6641. The Best Nontoxic Utensils To Replace Black Plastic Spatulas (2026)

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

More difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

New in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

There are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

The brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No

What we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

The same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

With five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That said, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

High-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

Not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

#6639. The Best Black Friday Jewelry Deals 2026, Handpicked by Vogue Editors

We love a good Black Friday fashion deal as much as the next. A cashmere sweater half off? A pair of boots we’ve been eyeing all season, at a fraction of its original price? Yes, and yes. But while the clothing (and home and beauty!) discounts are certainly worth browsing, we find the best Black Friday sales in the jewelry department.

Black Friday is the perfect opportunity to invest in the pieces you’ve been dreaming about but haven’t quite been able to justify buying at full price. Maybe it’s a diamond tennis necklace you’ve had on your wishlist for months, a pair of gold hoops you imagine you’ll never take off, or a delicate bracelet that will look just as good stacked with existing favorites as it does on its own. And while there’s certainly moments indulge in an impulse, jewelry is one category where planning pays off. Fine jewelry, in particular, adds up—so when our favorite brands offer a discount, we pay attention.

#6636. Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

While this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an important role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

But for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous New York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

#6635. Sarah Pidgeon Ticks Off Two of Winter’s Biggest Outerwear Trends in One Viral Coat

It’s been a banner year for Sarah Pidgeon’s outerwear wardrobe. The actor, who made her debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed list this week, has spent much of 2026 investing in a really good collection of coats. And while playing Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy in Love Story has furnished Pidgeon with an extensive knowledge of the late fashion publicist’s preferred ’90s silhouettes, her own tastes are often a little more irreverent and varied.

Taking in a Knicks and Cavaliers game at Madison Square Garden in New York this week, Pidgeon ticked off two of the season’s biggest outerwear trends—animal print and flourishes of faux fur, as well as the sophisticated standing collar shape—in one covetable coat. The actor wore the Dolly Maxi by Carelli, an elongated iteration of the label’s cult jacket, with cream-and-black spotted, pony hair-effect fabric, a jaw-grazing collar, and fluffy chocolate-brown cuffs. Pidgeon let the coat do most of the talking, adding straight-leg blue jeans, pointy black boots, and her trusty black Balenciaga Le City bag, which she clutched under her arm.

Carelli is one of the runaway fashion success stories of 2026. Founded by Anna Carels in early 2025, the brand has amassed a celebrity clientele that includes Dua Lipa, Olivia Dean, and Peggy Gou, as well as legions of fans on TikTok. As Carels told British Vogue earlier this month, the original Dolly sold out in under an hour. The designer’s penchant for old-school glamour chimes with a broader appetite for rather louche, vintage-inflected outerwear: See Conner Ives’s decadent fur-trimmed creations and Charlotte Simone’s always sell-out fuzzy numbers, as well as the proliferation of vintage silk opera coats on everyone from Kendall Jenner to Hailey Bieber and Jennifer Lawrence. After several seasons of austere and minimalist coats, we’re all in the mood for something a little more flamboyant. (Vogue’s predictions for the hottest coats of the coldest months says just as much.)

Pidgeon is no stranger to the timeless pleasures of a leopard-print coat. During her Love Story press tour, the actor stepped out in Adam Lippes’s leopard chenille Margaux coat in a subtle nod to Bessette-Kennedy’s own affinity for animal print. She’s also made a habit of punctuating her more pared-back outfits with leopard-print accessories.

Elsewhere in her enviable outerwear rotation? A collarless leather trench from Aflalo, a sculptural peplum jacket from Celine, and the supple Prada leathers she sported during fashion month.

Working with stylist Emma Jade Morrison, Pidgeon has struck an interesting balance between the restraint that characterized CBK’s wardrobe and her own more adventurous inclinations. She has an eye for younger labels, too, and a knack for assimilating their more idiosyncratic designs into an otherwise unfussy wardrobe of great denim, white tees, and ’90s-coded accessories. The Carelli coat feels especially at home among them. Consider Sarah Pidgeon’s latest outing some inspiration: swap out that sensible black winter coat in favor of something with a little more personality. Match point!

Not the one you bought in a rush for that wedding this summer, or the hand-me-down that fits badly, but not badly enough to get rid of. No, it’s time to say enough is enough: I am an adult, and I will own at least one suit that makes me look incredible, and feel even better than that.

And there really is no better time. Because while a discount on face wash might save you might save you four dollars, a 50% markdown on a suit—and yes, those currently exist—can save you hundreds, if not thousands of them. This is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

Whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.
