Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new study has rewritten the role of one of the brain's major speech hubs, opening new possibilities for treating people who can't communicate verbally due to brain damage.

The study, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Science, may help to solve a 150-year-old mystery in neuroscience.

Nowadays, neuroscientists use cutting-edge tools to tease apart the junctions and wiring of our complex brains. But some basic theories in the field are far from new and rest on past discoveries. One of those theories concerns how the brain produces and comprehends speech.

In the 1860s, German neuroanatomist Carl Wernicke identified an area of the brain that is critical to speech and usually found in the temporal lobe on the left side of the organ. Damage to Wernicke's area makes it challenging for people to understand what others are saying ‪—‬ a condition known as Wernicke's aphasia. Therefore, the brain region has been primarily thought of as a decoder that helps us break down the meaning of other people's speech.

Wernicke's area (red) is found in the left temporal lobe.

But that isn't the whole story. While people who have Wernicke's aphasia can speak in a normal cadence, the words they use don't match their intention. They might substitute semantically related words, with "shoe" becoming "foot," or they might mix up words that have similar sounds, like "leg" and "peg." This can make their sentences sound like nonsensical word salad and thus undermine patients' ability to communicate.

These symptoms make it clear that damage to Wernicke's area affects not just speech comprehension but also speech production. But neuroscientists couldn't identify how this function arose in the brain region or which cells contributed to it.

The question "has remained a mystery for over 150 years now," said study co-author Alexander Silva, a neuroscientist at the University of California, San Francisco.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One hypothesis is [that] it acts kind of like a proofreader. It listens to you speak, and it corrects errors," Silva explained. "But another is that there's actually dedicated activity in this area that generates upcoming speech."

In their new study, Silva and his colleagues set out to solve the conundrum, using a series of complementary tests that involved recording people's brain activity as they spoke. They had access to powerful tools for understanding brain function, like electrocorticography electrodes, which are implanted onto the brain's surface to measure neural activity. The precision of these tools enabled the team to investigate Wernicke's area at high temporal and spatial resolutions, Silva told Live Science.

The team recruited 28 participants with epilepsy, who already had electrodes implanted to monitor their seizures. They identified a small group of brain cells within Wernicke's area that fired about a quarter of a second before participants spoke words aloud. The signal seemed to be preparing for the speech production, and it could be separated from linked auditory signals made by cells responding to the resulting sound of the spoken words.

But this evidence alone couldn't prove that these cells actually caused speech; it could only correlate the signal with speech production. To connect the dots, the scientists mapped the brains of hundreds of people who were undergoing surgery to have temporal-lobe tumors removed and tested how the surgery affected their speech.

This analysis supported their previous findings; patients were much more likely to have trouble speaking after surgery if the procedure had damaged Wernicke's area, suggesting the area had a role in speech production.

We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why.

Finally, in 13 people with implanted electrodes and undamaged Wernicke's areas, the researchers tested what happened when they stimulated the brain. When the scientists sent a wave of electricity through the speech-preparation area just before participants opened their mouths to talk, the stimulation caused them to make word errors that resembled Wernicke's aphasia.

The researchers then moved on to a different question: Could these discoveries about Wernicke's area help people whose speech is affected by brain damage?

Using more electrode data, the team identified individual brain cells in Wernicke's area that were linked to saying particular words. Then, they looked at two patients with speech paralysis; these individuals were unable to speak after strokes damaged their brainstems and they'd had electrodes implanted in their brains that sent signals to brain-computer speech devices.

The devices which interpret signals from undamaged areas of the brain to spell out words the patients are trying to say onto a screen. In these patients, the scientists monitored activity from neurons in Wernicke's area with electrodes and were able to decode what the participants were attempting to communicate.

Silva said these discoveries rewrite the textbook on Wernicke's area. Adeen Flinker, a neuroscientist at New York University who was not involved in the study, agreed.

"We already knew that damage to Wernicke's area can lead to speech production errors, but this publication answers why," Flinker told Live Science.

The new findings could lead to better brain-computer interfaces for treating aphasia, Silva said. Until now, patients who have benefited from these interfaces have mainly had problems with the pathways linking their motor cortex and mouth muscles, he said, such as people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

"This is actually a small number of patients relative to the number of patients that have aphasia ‪—‬ so a language disorder from injury to the cortex itself," Silva said. These patients have vocal paralysis but are unable to benefit from BCIs because of this cortical damage, Flinker noted.

This special spot in Wernicke's area could be a new target for brain-computer interfaces aimed at helping patients with aphasia, Silva continued. "We really think that this is an area that could expand the number of people that could benefit from the technology in the near future," he concluded.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Silva, A. B., Leonard, M. K., Hullett, P. W., Levy, D. F., Wang, C., Xu, D., Bhaya-Grossman, I., & Chang, E. F. (2026). A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke's area. Science, 394(6826). https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef8963

#6552. Citrus Madeleines

Marcel Proust and madeleines are so intrinsically linked that in France, a madeleine de Proust has become a common expression used to describe a smell, sound, or taste that brings back old memories. Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. Freezing the pan and placing it on a hot sheet pan will make the bump pop even more!

As much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

Put ½ cup / 115 g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat and melt, stirring and scraping the bottom with a rubber spatula, until the foaming subsides and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and the milk solids are golden brown, 5–7 minutes. Scrape the melted butter and milk solids into a small heatproof bowl and refrigerate until the butter is solid and creamy.

Sift together 1 cup / 125 g all-purpose flour, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ¼ tsp. salt in a small bowl and set aside.

Add ½ cup / 100 g light brown sugar to a small bowl and rub the sugar with zest of 1 Cara Cara orange. Combine the sugar, 1 Tbsp. honey, and 2 eggs in the bowl of a stand mixer, fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk for 2 minutes on medium-low speed, then increase the speed to medium-high and whisk for another 5–6 minutes, until very pale and airy.

Add the cooled butter to the egg mixture while whisking on low speed, then fold in the flour mixture until just combined.

Transfer the batter to an airtight container and refrigerate for at least 6 hours but preferably overnight.

Grease a madeleine pan with unsalted butter, then dust with all-purpose flour and knock out any excess. Place the pan in the freezer for at least an hour.

Use a 1-Tbsp. measure or transfer the cold batter to a piping bag and fill the center of each cup with 20 g of batter (three-quarters full, or a little more than 1 Tbsp.). Refrigerate the madeleine pan for 1 hour.

Place a sheet pan in the oven and preheat the oven to 350°F / 180°C.

Place the madeleine pan directly on the hot sheet pan and bake for 10–13 minutes, until the madeleines are golden brown and their signature bump springs back when pressed lightly.

Tap the tray to release the cakes and immediately turn out onto a wire rack to cool, turning them bump-side up.

Whisk together ¼ cup / 30 g powdered sugar and ¾ tsp. ground coriander in a small bowl and dust over the warm madeleines.

#6549. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft just reached 1 light-day from our planet, but a newfound glitch in the probe's onboard computer is preventing it from sharing science data with Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has confirmed that its Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a record-breaking 1 light-day from Earth — but new milestones come with old problems.

On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem.

But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction.

"We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, said at a NASA news conference Thursday, adding that she is "confident" that the science data will continue flowing again soon.

Using the carrier signal, the team confirmed that the probe had reached its latest distance milestone of 1 light-day from Earth, or roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away, Wednesday (Nov. 18). At this distance, which no human-made object had ever reached before, it takes a full 24 hours for radio signals traveling at the speed of light to get from Earth to Voyager 1 and vice versa. (The spacecraft's twin probe, Voyager 2, is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035.)

This incredible distance, coupled with the spacecraft's five-decade-old hardware, makes troubleshooting problems on the probe extremely arduous, Dodd explained.

An illustration depicting Voyager 1 at one light-day from Earth.

"It takes two days to diagnose anything with the spacecraft — so we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low," she said. "We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to NASA, the current glitch likely stems from Voyager's onboard computer, which is responsible for collecting data from its science instruments and transmitting it back to Earth in a readable format. The team encountered a similar problem in November 2023 that prevented Voyager 1 from sharing science data until engineers solved the issue in June 2024. The mission team is approaching this new glitch the same way they solved the previous one, NASA wrote in a blog post.

If the fix succeeds, Voyager 1 will continue transmitting data from its two remaining science instruments — a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields in interstellar space, and a plasma wave detector, which measures charged particles in the interstellar medium. To conserve power on the aging spacecraft, the mission team shut off some of Voyager's instruments earlier this year while powering other, more efficient ones in a "Big Bang" maneuver that should keep the probe alive through at least 2027.

We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age

However, it's only a matter of time before Voyager 1 runs out of juice and closes its mechanical eyes to the cosmos. After that, it will continue drifting through interstellar space indefinitely, carrying a Golden Record of images, music and information about life on Earth. In the meantime, Voyager will continue learning everything it can about the strange environment of the interstellar medium — the space between stars, where only Voyagers 1 and 2 have ever been before.

Voyager 1 officially reached interstellar space in 2012, after transforming our views of Jupiter, Saturn and other solar system bodies. For more about the probe's incredible discoveries, check out our collection of Voyager 1's iconic photos.

#6546. Striped Malted Pound Cake

My earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

This cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

Transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

In a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

#6545. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

This beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

Pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights company HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

We’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the company is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

The biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

#6542. This Clever Fork Trick Makes Slicing Cheese So Much Easier

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

Start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

#6540. Thanksgiving Cornbread

Traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

#6539. Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

For the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really important to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Recently, Live Science asked its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with, based on a new study that leveraged AI to decode different vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recently, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the different vocalizations of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), bringing scientists one step closer to talking to animals.

Birds are just some of many animals that experts hope to understand and communicate with. Scientists are also deciphering the clicks and calls of sperm whales and humpback whales. Some animals, like cats, can change their meows depending on what they're seeking from their owners, such as food or attention.

In the wake of Elie's new findings, Live Science asked its readers what animal they would want to talk to if they could.

Over 550 people voted in our poll, with 54% picking dog. The next-largest voting group, 28% of respondents, chose cat.

The comments reflected the obvious trend of readers wanting to speak to their pets. One commenter wrote, "Cats, simply because I've had more of them as pets over the decades than anything else. I don't think spiders would be interesting conversationalists, I'm unlikely to encounter whales here in the middle of North America, and dogs that I meet on my daily walks are only invested in the canine treats I carry."

Another reader said we'd never be able to understand our pets even if we could communicate with them. "Unfortunately you would have to experience the world through your nose to truly understand what they experience. To understand what a dog is thinking you would have to 'be' a dog. A problem with communicating with any non-human being, whether it be octopi, whale, cat or extra terrestrial. It seems to be a human thing that people can't just sit, observe and interpret the world around them as it is. Everything needs to be explained!"

Not everyone chose cats and dogs, though. One reader wrote, "I would want to know my horse's backstory."

Several other commenters mentioned octopuses, with one commenter saying, "I’m disappointed that octopi weren't included on the list. I've read that they are incredibly intelligent, interact with humans and are able to think and plan. Also they can shape shift and change color and patterns. I love my dogs but I don't imagine they are capable of matching the observations and conversations octopi might have."

Do you agree or disagree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6537. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

#6536. Giant Sheet-Pan Chocolate Almond Croissant

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

This giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

Meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

Yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

Serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

#6534. Victoria Beckham Pre-Fall 2027

Victoria Beckham is at her best when she’s talking through her fashion specifics. “These are sand-washed silk,” she’s saying of the pair of flowy ivory trousers that, paired with a bomber jacket, stride across the first shot in her pre-collection lookbook. “I love how you have this utilitarian style, but because it’s in beautiful silk, it’s fluid and very light. These materials are so great,” she added. “Because we can layer them at the time of year in which the collection is available, May through October.”

There’s no fluff or padding around Beckham’s focus on what works; she’s essentially honed it down to the practical elegance of her tailoring and city daywear on the one hand, and her fluttery, deconstructed evening dresses on the other. Consistency and careful attention to fit and sizing are underestimated loyalty-generators in today’s fashion-sphere. Plus, in the challenging circumstances thrown at us in today’s climate—both the literal heat forecast for next summer, and the tough financial one—there’s the obvious (though astonishingly overlooked) merit in making clothes that pass both of these stringent tests.

Thus, she’s pairing lightly deconstructed trench coat derivatives, bombers, parkas, and apparently spontaneously-belted jackets with apricot denim workwear-ish jeans, the trick being that it comes off as a way of dressing that’s a kind of easy, personalized collage to swap around day-by-day. Perhaps that’s what she meant when she said that she’d been looking at Cindy Sherman: all these roles and disguises we take on, something else that women take into account as they’re designing.

The appearance of effortless clarity without being over-prescriptive is the VB way. Her tailoring will be familiar, also a good thing for return customers. Why mess with the success of a signature blazer cut with a low clean, diagonal closure? “I never like tailoring that is too feminine, but I love the lightness that we’ve got here,” she pointed out. The differences within this high summer collection are in the linen fabrications, and in a new, skinny-leg trouser. The ankle hem has a zip in it.

Beckham’s been seen out and about pioneering that look lately, as well as the illusory ‘double-fronted’ tuxedo jacket she wore recently to a gig by her musician son Cruz. Modernized slip dress columns and draped tea-dress midis are also looks Beckham’s practiced as part of her public-fronting persona over the years. Will there be people who buy into all this purely as fans who want to dress like a celebrity? Yes, certainly. But women of Beckham’s generation are wise and seasoned consumers who know from long experience how often the image of a look dismally fails to deliver in the cold light of a changing room.

Beckham’s success has been in dedicating herself to closing that credibility gap, while building out the credibility of her cosmetics brand. Clothes and accessories-wise, her highly effective economy of style (and her considerate sizing) makes it all add up to a growing commercial phenomenon. All of that’s being reflected in the enthusiastic reaction to the opening of the Victoria Beckham New York store this year. “Consequently, the collections are growing, which is really great for us,” she said. “We are smashing through all the targets that we set, so we know that there is a real opportunity for us in retail expansion, which is what I said was the plan for this year. So we’re continuing on that mission next year, already looking at different locations in different territories.”

#6533. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#6532. I Tried Ina Garten’s Ranch Dressing, and It Changed My Mind About Ranch

I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

Add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

That’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is important, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

The first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

And the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

By the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6529. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

No ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

#6528. The Best Black Friday Meal Kit Deals Offer Deep Discounts

It’s no surprise that BA editors love to cook, and considering you’re on our site right now, we’re willing to guess you do too. But life can get hectic, especially in the lead-up to the end of the year. That’s where meal kits come in: Think of them as a dinnertime helping hand—everything you need to get a hot meal on the table is delivered in a single box. And during the Black Friday sales bonanza, many of these services are available at a discount.

Some of the best meal kits according to our years of extensive testing—including the best affordable meal kits and some of our favorite meal kits for families—have Cyber Week offers running. Each of these services offers a weekly menu (so you can take a break from meal-planning), and includes options for a range of dietary needs, whether you're following a low-carb, gluten-free, dairy-free, Paleo, or pescatarian eating style. And if fully-prepared heat-and-eat meals are more your speed, we found deals on those, too.

Want excellent, chef-designed prepared meals delivered to your door? One of our absolute favorite meal delivery services is CookUnity. It specializes in pre-cooked meals that you heat in the oven or microwave when you're ready to eat. But these aren't your average re-heatable dinners. All the dishes are unique and made by chefs across the country—think recipes like Desi Butter Chicken with Cauliflower Mash and Roasted Peri-Peri Chicken with Harissa Brussels Sprouts.

If you're already salivating, trust us—we're right there with you. You can satiate the craving at a discount this Black Friday with a whole 50% off your first order. Just use code BONAPPCU50.

HelloFresh offers great portion sizes, easy-to-cook meals, and over 100 weekly menu and market items to choose from. It's great for single- or dual-person households, and people who can't commit to using a whole bulb of garlic with pre-portioned ingredients and super clear steps. Through Cyber Monday, you can get 10 free meals and a free Staub ceramic baking dish (which will come with your third box) to help make dinner prep even easier.

Green Chef sets itself apart by offering organic ingredients and sticking to a sustainability pledge that has the brand offsetting its delivery emissions and plastic use. For Black Friday/Cyber Monday, they’re offering 50% off your first box and 20% off your next two months of orders.

You can’t go wrong with a meal kit like Blue Apron, one of the OGs in the space. The promise is similar to HelloFresh: pre-portioned ingredients and straightforward instructions that'll have you making healthy and delicious meals at home with ease.

Purple Carrot is a fully plant-based meal kit delivery service that offers both premade meals and meal kits for you to prep. Multiple BA staffers and contributors have tried it many times throughout the years, and it's consistently fared well in our product tests. Proof? This review from contributor Carina Finn: “I never missed the meat in a Purple Carrot meal. I even found myself getting legitimately excited about my “healthy dinner at home” nights—especially since I didn’t have to grocery shop.”

For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, they’re offering new customers 50% off their order plus free shipping. Use code 50FORME to redeem the discount, which is valid on all orders over $65.

If you love cooking but don't have time for all of the planning, prep, and shopping required to put together satisfying home-cooked meals, try Marley Spoon. The service uses recipes from Martha Stewart herself and still requires you to do at least some of the chopping and dicing to making your meal. The recipes even recommend a few cooking tricks to use in your everyday life.

Parents and caregivers who want to skimp on shopping and prep without skimping on nutrition will love Little Spoon—a meal kit specifically for feeding babies, toddlers, and little kids. The service will ship ready-to-heat-and-eat meals (and snacks!) that are chef- and dietician-approved. For Black Friday, save 60% on your first order with the code EARLYBIRD60 through 11/26, and 65% on your first order with code SAVEBIG65 from 11/27–12/01.

#6527. Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling)

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.
