#6526. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, New York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.)

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she says. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, says that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to new takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

#6525. Jif’s Surprising New Product at Costco Has Nothing to Do with Sandwiches

Hold the jelly! The iconic peanut butter brand is taking a surprisingly savory direction with its latest product.

Who says peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

Jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Some locations of the warehouse retailer are now carrying a six-pack of Jif stir-fry-style instant ramen noodles, giving shoppers an entirely different way to enjoy the taste of peanut butter.

But so far, the reviews among shoppers are mixed.

“Anyone who thinks this sounds gross has never had Thai food and it shows. Peanut butter noodles are kinda awesome,” one fan wrote in a video making the rounds on Instagram.

“Prolly fire w some chili oil,” another claimed.

“I had this last month. Pretty good for instant noodles,” another said.

A fourth wrote, “As a peanut butter [connoisseur] I don’t approve this.”

“Diabolical waste of resources,” a fifth claimed.

Peanuts have long been incorporated into savory noodle dishes, particularly in Asian-inspired cooking. Still, seeing the recognizable Jif logo on a package of instant noodles might have you raising your eyebrows. Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

Jif has another product worth keeping an eye out for at Costco. The brand’s peanut butter and chocolate pretzel Snappers hit shelves in October and offer a sweet-and-salty alternative for those who aren’t quite sold on the noodles.

As always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?

During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried.

Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement. These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K.

The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected with the occupant of the famous ship burial.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," Wainwright said. In particular, experts have tried to work out who was buried in the "great ship burial" at Sutton Hoo. That person may have been King Rædwald, who ruled a kingdom in East Anglia and died around A.D. 627. The ship burial also contained an intricate and striking helmet. But the archaeologists are trying to learn more about the everyday East Anglians with the 2025 dig, which "moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants," Wainwright said.

During the last week of the month-long excavation, the team unearthed the unusual sand body burial. Accompanying the deceased were grave goods, including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, according to the statement. But directly underneath the sand body, the team found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," Wainwright said. Experts think the sand bodies and cremations discovered in the burial ground may predate the famous ship burial.

In the first episode of a four-part Time Team series on Sutton Hoo, which launched on YouTube on Nov. 14, experts found new evidence that the people buried in the Garden Field cemetery were acquiring wealth and increasing their social status — so much so that they buried at least one person with a gold ingot.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also investigated the possible remains of a dock that was used to build and launch ships into the River Deben and found an unusual fragment of a cremation urn that surprised the archaeologists because it was decorated rather than plain.

"Well, it's at Sutton Hoo. Anything can happen," Justin Garner-Lahire, managing director at FAS Heritage, said in the video.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6521. Herby Cottage Cheese Scones

These garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant. I typically hydrate scones with cream or buttermilk, but in this case I use cottage cheese, giving the scones a sort of 1970s vintage feel. Cottage cheese is made by curdling milk with an acid, like vinegar or lemon juice, which separates the curds from the whey. The curds are then drained, rinsed to remove excess acidity, and sometimes mixed with cream. It may seem unusual to stir this retro breakfast staple into your scone dough, but it creates a tender, flavorful crumb that stays moist long after baking.

This is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs. In addition to Sonora or other soft wheat flour, I use refined all-­purpose flour and fine yellow cornmeal. You’ll find yourself mincing herbs to add to the mix. Make sure to use a sharp chef’s knife that won’t bruise the herby bits; this helps them retain their flavor and aroma. Roasting the scallions softens and caramelizes them a bit. I also add lemon zest and cracked black pepper. Both play a supporting role, never overpowering the herbs. To finish, garnish with a few flakes of crunchy salt, such as Maldon.

Smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea. They also pair perfectly with smoked salmon or egg salad. For an elegant appetizer, they can be baked into smaller versions of themselves (see the variation that follows).

Variation: Cocktail SconesTo make cocktail scones, divide the dough into 3 equal portions and pat each down into a disk about 4" (10 cm) in diameter and ¾" (2 cm) thick. Cut each disk into 8 wedges. Finish as directed in the main recipe. You’ll end up with 24 mini scones. Bake on two baking sheets for 12 minutes, then rotate the sheets and switch their positions in the oven. Bake for another 10–12 minutes, until golden.

Place an oven rack in the middle position and preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).

Place 6 scallions on a rimmed baking sheet and drizzle with 1 Tbsp. olive oil. Roast until tender, 6–8 minutes. When the bulb part of a scallion can be easily pierced with a paring knife, the scallions are ready. Let them cool completely. Trim the roots and tops, leaving all the white part and 2" (5 cm) of the green part, and chop them roughly.

Increase the oven temperature to 400°F (205°C). Line another rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.

Combine ⅔ cup (85 g) whole-­grain all-purpose wheat flour, ⅔ cup (90 g) all-­purpose flour, ½ cup (65 g) fine cornmeal, 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. kosher salt in a mixing bowl. Add ½ cup (112 g/1 stick/4 oz.) cold unsalted butter, cut into ½" (1.25 cm) cubes, and toss to combine. Quickly cut the butter cubes into the dry ingredients by pinching the butter with your fingertips—­imagine you’re snapping your fingers—­until the mixture resembles a coarse meal with butter pieces the size of cornflakes. Add the scallions, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh dill, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh chives, 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest, and ¼ tsp. freshly cracked black pepper and toss to combine.

Using your hands, make a well in the center of the mixture. Whisk 1¼ cups (295 ml) 4% cottage cheese with 1 large egg and a dash of hot sauce and pour into the well. Toss gently with both hands (as if tossing a salad) until a rough dough is formed.

To shape the scones, transfer the dough to a lightly floured surface. Pat it down into a disk about 6" (15 cm) in diameter and 1" (2.5 cm) thick. Using a large chef’s knife, slice into 10 equal wedges (as you would a cake or a pie).

Transfer each individual scone to the prepared baking sheet, placing them at least 2" (5 cm) apart. Brush with 1 large beaten egg, then season with a sprinkle of coarse sea salt and black pepper. Bake for 10 minutes, then rotate the baking sheet and bake for another 10–12 minutes, until the edges of the scones are golden. These are delicious while still warm, but you can also serve them at room temperature.

#6520. Sticky Miso Chicken

Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Anthropic mathematician using Claude claims to have proven the most famous problem in math — the Riemann hypothesis — in the latest, but potentially most consequential, example of artificial intelligence (AI) producing stunning math results.

AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter.

Without this shift, we risk drowning genuine insight in a flood of plausible but poorly understood mathematics.

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're putting out for free. If you liked this story, please consider subscribing.

Mathematical judgment is the ability to distinguish a result that is correct, but boring, from one that might fundamentally change how we think about the problem or even the whole area of mathematics surrounding the problem.

AI could generate hundreds of thousands of complex variations on a theorem, but these variations might add very little to mathematical knowledge, each one ultimately proving a dead end. A truly consequential result might settle a long-standing unsolved problem or connect to apparently unrelated areas. It is mathematical judgment that allows us to tell the difference between the two.

Earlier this year, an OpenAI system produced a counterexample to the long-standing planar unit distance problem, overturning a conjecture of Paul Erdős that had resisted mathematicians for decades. More recently, OpenAI announced an apparent solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a celebrated question about whether equations describing fluid flow can develop singularities, or infinite values. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems — a set of seven well-known and complex math problems, each with a $1 million prize attached.

Whether OpenAI's result ultimately stands up to scrutiny remains to be seen. But what is clear is that AI systems are now operating at a level that many mathematicians did not expect to witness for years, if not decades. OpenAI has since released hundreds of further mathematical results, leaving mathematicians scrambling to assess their correctness and significance.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This does not mean that mathematicians are about to become obsolete. But it does mean we need to carefully reconsider what their precise purpose is.

Traditionally, expertise has been closely associated with production: Experts solve difficult problems, prove theorems, construct models and write papers. If AI can generate proofs, conjectures and probe research areas at unprecedented speed and scale, mathematical production is no longer necessarily the bottleneck. Instead, many pure mathematicians would argue that it is mathematical judgment that will become the scarcer resource.

Human judgment remains necessary because proofs generated by AI are not necessarily illuminating, comprehensible or even reliable. Some proofs may be so long or opaque that checking them requires substantial work by specialists and even more work to reinterpret them in a way that is meaningful to human mathematicians.

A proof can be valid without offering insight into why it is true or how its ideas might be employed elsewhere. The job of human mathematicians will be to become arbiters of the correctness of proofs, but also to scrutinize the reasoning and to extract the underlying ideas, determining whether the result says anything that meaningfully advances the field.

Mathematics, as a research community, needs to react rapidly to this change. Mathematicians and journals must prioritize significance over output. Mathematics involves deciding which results are important as well as generating them. A proof can be correct without being insightful. To give a simplified example, AI might "prove" that the square of a number divisible by two is divisible by four and then prove that the square of a number divisible by three is divisible by nine, and so on with ever larger integers. However, each new "proof" isn't an example of insightful mathematics, just a variation on the same elementary idea.

AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

In contrast, a significant proof might settle a long-standing question, reveal an unexpected connection between disparate fields or develop a technique which is useful in the solution of many other problems.

Journals should therefore require authors to explain clearly what is genuinely new, why it matters — and what role AI played. Reviewers should judge whether a result deepens understanding, rather than merely verifying that the argument works. That does not mean rejecting work whose eventual importance is uncertain. The history of mathematics is full of ideas whose significance became apparent only decades later, so journals must continue to make room for foundational, exploratory and curiosity-driven research.

But there is a difference between a result with as-yet unknown implications and one that is unlikely ever to be insightful. Mathematical judgement cannot guarantee that nothing valuable is ever overlooked. It can, however, distinguish work that contains genuinely new ideas or possibilities from the automated production of uninteresting dead ends.

Universities and funders should also stop treating publication counts as a convenient proxy for quality. Careers are built around papers, citations, grants and prizes, but these measures were developed when producing sophisticated mathematics demanded substantial human time and effort. In the age of AI, work that might previously have taken years of careful thought could now be produced in weeks or even days.

Consequently, as the cost of generating mathematical results falls dramatically, those measures of quality become less useful. A decreased reliance on traditional metrics may be no bad thing, but institutions need credible alternatives: assessments of a researcher's most important contributions, evidence of intellectual leadership and explanations of how their work has changed understanding. This is urgent because mathematicians are already struggling to evaluate the sheer volume of material being produced.

Finally, mathematical training must continue to reward understanding. Written work alone will become a less reliable guide to individual capability when papers, reports and applications can be written mostly using AI. Seminars, discussions and collaborations can reveal whether someone understands an argument, can defend it and can connect it to other ideas. Demonstrating understanding has always been a more important quality in university students than simply presenting the answer; education and recruitment should now reflect that principle more explicitly.

Critics might argue that this is an overreaction. Mathematical claims still require proof, peer review already evaluates significance, and AI is simply another tool, like a calculator or computer algebra system. There is a degree of truth to each objection. Yet the explosion in the number of published papers changes the nature of the game. A calculator does not generate hundreds of research claims that specialists must spend precious time checking. AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

Recent advances have understandably generated both excitement and anxiety. The right response is neither to reject AI nor to unguardedly celebrate every finding it produces. Journals, universities and funders should adapt their incentives now, before quantity overwhelms judgment completely.

In an environment increasingly capable of automatically generating research-level mathematics, the most valuable experts will be those who know which questions are worth asking, which results deserve trust and which ideas are worth our attention.

#6516. Why Pizza Has Become an Unofficial Thanksgiving Tradition

Turkey gets Thursday, but Wednesday is all about the 'za.

It’s Thanksgiving Eve. The turkey is hogging an entire fridge shelf, every baking dish is spoken for and the cousins just pulled into the driveway. Then somebody asks what’s for dinner, and the only reasonable answer comes in a cardboard box.

If that sounds familiar, you’re in excellent company. As it turns out, the night before the big feast is one of the busiest times of the year for pizza orders, and our collective craving for a good slice is practically a holiday tradition of its own.

Ridiculously popular. According to DoorDash’s latest trends report, pizza was the No. 1 pick this time last year, with orders jumping more than 50% compared with other Wednesdays in November. And the ‘za of choice? Plain cheese, up a whopping 70%.

The craze isn’t limited to the couch, either. Toast data shows that pizza orders at sit-down restaurants and bars spiked 48% that evening. Salads, meanwhile, dipped 5%, which sounds about right.

National chains feel the rush, too. “Across the industry, it consistently lands in the top handful alongside Halloween and the Super Bowl,” Greg Hamilton, chief marketing officer at Little Caesars, said in a statement.

There’s a certain satisfaction in wiping down the counters the day before, knowing the casseroles are assembled and you’re as ready for tomorrow as you’ll ever be. The last thing anyone wants to do is pull another pan out of the cupboard.

“Thanksgiving Eve is about making life easier,” Hamilton said. “The kitchen is already prepped for Thursday, the house is filling up and nobody wants to cook twice.”

But there’s more to it than giving the dishwasher a break. College kids are back in their hometowns, and childhood friends are making plans to reunite. Even siblings who usually communicate via memes in the family group chat are finally in the same room.

With AAA expecting 81.5 million Americans to travel this week, plenty of those reunions kick off a day before anyone carves anything. Order pizza, and whoever’s hosting actually hears the surprise engagement announcement instead of yelling “Wait, WHAT?” over a sizzling skillet.

Most customers “tend to go with the classics,” Hamilton noted, but if you’re looking to shake up your usual order (or feed a small army without spending a fortune), several pizza chains have specials running right now:

Prices and participation vary by location, and given how busy tonight is shaping up to be, ordering ahead isn’t a bad idea.

Is your crew ordering in before turkey day or cooking two nights in a row? Let us know in the comments below!

#6515. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

#6514. Turkey in Mole Poblano

It may be called the great American bird, but turkey was first domesticated in Mexico, where, as James Beard once wrote, “it was to that country what beef is to the United States.” One of chef Rick Bayless’s favorite preparations is a celebratory dish from the Mexican state of Puebla: a slow braise of breast meat in a deep, dark mole that’s shot through with three kinds of dried chiles, studded with peanuts and pumpkin seeds, and enriched with chocolate and spices. The spicy, sweet, savory sauce can be sopped up with hot tortillas and rice, or even crusty bread.

It may be called the great American bird, but turkey was first domesticated in Mexico, where, as James Beard once wrote, “it was to that country what beef is to the United States.” One of chef Rick Bayless’s favorite preparations is a celebratory dish from the Mexican state of Puebla: a slow braise of breast meat in a deep, dark mole that’s shot through with three kinds of dried chiles, studded with peanuts and pumpkin seeds, and enriched with chocolate and spices. The spicy, sweet, savory sauce can be sopped up with hot tortillas and rice, or even crusty bread.

#6513. The Safest Way to Handle a Kitchen Grease Fire

A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

One of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

That respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

What makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

Whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s important to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s important to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

Should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

The most important thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

Both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:

If covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s important to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

#6512. Pickled Celery Gibson

Traditionally, a Gibson is a savory twist on a martini, substituting a cocktail onion for the olive. My version, which incorporates the very easy homemade Pickled Celery, has the same clean, briny qualities as the classic but with a touch of complexity from the pickling spices and a bright, leafy flavor. I like to stir my Gibson with a handful of celery leaves to amp up that fresh flavor, but if your celery is leafless, or if you’re making this for a big group, feel free to exclude that ingredient.

From Victorian celery vases to midcentury relish trays, celery has been part of hosting parties in the United States for many generations. At gatherings hosted by my grandma Dorothy in western New York in the ’90s, I remember big stalks of celery resting in pitchers of salt water in the middle of every table, acting as both a palate-cleansing snack and a centerpiece. Similarly, this recipe for pickled celery can function as a garnish (consider skewering it onto a cocktail pick with a cornichon and a cherry tomato for a Bloody Mary), part of a canapé, or just as a snack on its own.

In a small saucepan over low heat, combine ½ cup [120 ml] distilled vinegar, 1 tsp. kosher salt, 1 tsp. sugar, 2 garlic cloves, 1 tsp. black peppercorns, 1 clove, and ¼ tsp. coriander seeds with ½ cup [120 ml] water. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the sugar and salt are dissolved. Place 4 celery stalks (about 200 g), cut into 1½" [4 cm] lengths, in a heatproof bowl, and pour the hot brine over it. Allow the mixture to cool to room temperature, then transfer it to an airtight container. Refrigerate at least overnight before using, and store, refrigerated, for up to 1 week.

Place a coupe, Nick and Nora, or martini glass in the freezer to chill.

Add 2½ oz. [75 ml] gin, ½ oz. [15 ml] dry vermouth, ½ oz. [15 ml] brine from Pickled Celery, and 1 small handful of celery leaves (if using) to a cocktail mixing glass (or a sturdy jar) with a handful of ice cubes. Using a cocktail spoon, stir vigorously for 30 seconds, or until the outside of the glass feels extremely cold.

Strain into the chilled glass, garnish with 1 piece Pickled Celery on a cocktail pick, and serve.

#6511. Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

#6509. I Tried Dolly Parton’s Appalachian Apple Stack Cake, and It’s One-of-a-Kind

This warmly spiced cake from Dolly Parton can be made days in advance and is the perfect addition to your holiday dessert table.

All the adjectives I imagine to describe Dolly Parton, I can also attribute to this one-of-a-kind cake from her cookbook. It’s unlike anything I have ever made before, but at the same time it is warm and comforting, all while standing tall in a class by itself. With scents of apple, vanilla, cinnamon and allspice, it’s certainly a recipe to try this time of year and could even be a great addition to a Dolly-inspired meal.

An apple stack cake is a popular Appalachian dessert comprised of layers of spiced cake and apple filling. Dolly’s version uses molasses in the “crust,” aka cake layers and fresh apples in the filling (whereas other recipes often call for dried apples).

The original recipe for Dolly’s apple stack “cake” was actually referred to as a “pie” in her 1986 cookbook Dollywood Presents Tennessee Mountain Home Cooking. I wasn’t exactly sure why there was a crisscrossing of names until I started to prepare this unique recipe. The flour and butter in the “crust” layers are cut together using a pastry blender, much like you might do when making a traditional pie crust. Then, eggs, molasses, sugar, milk and spices are also added. This transforms the recipe into a thicker batter, similar to a scone or even a quick bread. The filling is like a thick, spiced applesauce with a thin layer spread between each stack.

I found the directions in the original recipe to be a bit confusing. For example, there was no mention of using cold butter even though the dough starts off more like pastry crust. In the instructions below, I added a bit more detail in order to clarify the process for anyone who wants to try making this special Dolly dessert.

In a large bowl, sift together flour and baking soda. Cut the cold butter into cubes and then use a pastry blender to cut the cubes into the flour mixture until it looks like coarse sand. In a separate bowl, beat together eggs, molasses, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon and milk.

Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture and mix until it looks like a thick dough. Cover the bottom of 6 round cake pans with parchment. Grease and flour the cake pans. Evenly divide the dough among the cake pans and, with floured hands, press it out toward the edges of each pan.

Bake at 300°F for 10 to 15 minutes, or until golden brown. Cool in the pans for 10 minutes, then remove to a wire rack and continue cooling.

Cook the apples slowly in water until soft. Strain any remaining liquid. This should yield about 1 cup of pulp. Add sugar, cinnamon and allspice. Cook over low heat until the sugar dissolves and the mixture thickens.

Place the filling between layers, and stack one layer on top of the other. This recipe will make two 3-layer cakes or one 6-layer cake. This cake is best after it sits for two or three days. Dust with powdered sugar before serving, if desired. Yield: 10 to 12 servings.

I was glad I did a little research before making this recipe to learn that it’s best to add parchment to the bottom of each cake pan to avoid sticking. Because I did this, the layers released easily from the pans, so I highly recommend this step. I also took a tip from the Taste of Home Apple Stack Cake recipe to add powdered sugar on top before serving. Since this cake needed a little something to finish off the look, this was just the right move. Plus, I doubt Dolly would disagree with a little extra accessorizing!

I agree that this recipe tastes best after it sits for a couple of days. The flavor of the molasses in the batter melds with the warm spices to create a dessert that is truly in a class by itself. Given that it can be made in advance, that is a great way to get a head start on a holiday meal and enjoy a stress-free treat that is already done and ready to enjoy. Serve with a scoop of ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream!

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, astronomers have caught two stars — a supergiant and a star slightly smaller than the sun — in the act of merging. After orbiting each other for thousands of years, the pair came together in just under seven years — a span short enough that researchers could watch the drama play out from start to finish. The discovery was described in a study published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

"Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, said in a NASA statement. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do."

The stars' imminent merger was originally picked up by NASA's now-retired Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer — a spacecraft that was designed to spot asteroids but also discovered many other interesting changes in the night sky.

Researchers noticed that a previously stable binary star system in the Andromeda galaxy, the closest major galaxy to ours, had begun to brighten. Follow-up observations from the Wide-Field Infrared Transient Explorer ‪—‬ a near-infrared instrument at the Palomar Observatory in California — revealed that the galaxy had also started spewing dust. Karambelkar’s team backed up these observations with data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in December 2025.

The researchers dubbed the binary pair "Bao" (after its formal name, AT 2025abao) and started keeping tabs. They found that sometime in 2018, the smaller component of Bao bumped into the surface of the supergiant Bao. From there, things escalated quickly. The stars started exchanging gas in a process known as common envelope evolution. The larger Bao dragged its smaller companion closer and closer, until it was finally sucked into the supergiant's core, releasing a gigantic burst of energy.

Views of the stellar merger in Andromeda (left) captured by the NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and James Webb space telescopes (right).

This dramatic culmination was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," study co-author Kishalay De, an astronomer at Columbia University, said in the statement.

The researchers were surprised by not only the speed of this interaction but also its outcome. Bao could have easily exploded into a supernova, transformed into a neutron star or collapsed into a black hole. Instead, it seems to have settled back into a single massive star. Future observations will give scientists a sense of how the new, rejuvenated Bao is holding up after its act of cosmic cannibalism.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team's analysis could also help inform future studies of supergiant stars and binary systems. Getting a clearer picture of how common envelope evolution works could allow astronomers to reconstruct how previous mergers went down. Thanks to NASA's new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, Karambelkar predicts Bao will be far from the last merging stars scientists spot.

Joanna Thompson is a science journalist and runner based in New York. #6507. This Is the Number One Cheese You Need on Your Holiday Cheese Board (No, It’s Not Cheddar)

I chatted with two cheesemongers to find out exactly what I should be putting on my cheese spreads this holiday season. Surprisingly, a classic cheddar isn't at the top!

After playing Tetris in my oven an hour before a holiday party, I’m always relieved I decided to serve a cheese board as the appetizer. Cheese boards don’t require much time to put together (and take up zero oven space), but I seem to linger on the cheese selection, always asking myself the same question: Which cheeses would everyone like to eat?

So, I sat down with the experts: Molly Browne, dean of mongers at Cheese State University and education director at Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin, and Emilia D’Albero, the first American ever crowned World’s Best Cheesemonger. They gave me the scoop on putting together the perfect holiday cheese board. Molly and Emilia recommend three to five cheeses per board, representing a variety of milk types, styles and flavors.

But which cheese should I buy that everyone would like? More specifically, what feels indulgent but won’t alienate picky eaters? I expected Molly and Emilia to recommend some extremely specific, hard-to-find cheeses, but both suggested varieties I could pick up at the grocery store.

According to Molly, the best cheese for a holiday cheese board that appeals to all ages is butterkase. This semi-firm cow’s milk cheese is creamy, smooth, relatively mild and exceptionally buttery—hence its German name, which translates to “butter cheese.” (If you’re as chronically online as I am, you may have heard of butterkase from @courtneycookinsta, who famously stuffs butterkase in a warm sweet potato and eats it for lunch.)

Butterkase is typically aged for only about a month, so it doesn’t have much funk, making it approachable for the under-10 and over-60 crowd. “I’ve seen my own child pick up a piece of it and eat it like an apple on multiple occasions,” says Molly. But because of butterkase’s slight complexity, Molly explained that it won’t leave those in the middle feeling devoid of flavor or a good eating experience, so it’s a safe bet for a charcuterie board.

Butterkase is made in Wisconsin and sold nationwide, but if you’re having trouble finding it, Gouda is a good alternative, especially Emilia’s recommendation: aged Gouda.

Aged Gouda is a Dutch-style hard cheese that matures anywhere from nine months to five years. As Gouda matures, the soft paste turns firm and speckles with those irresistible crunchy crystals. It takes on an indulgent butterscotch flavor, with subtle tropical notes, so it’s on the sweeter side. The longer the Gouda ages, the more intense those characteristics become. “In my experience, nobody’s ever turned down an aged Gouda,” says Emilia.

Because it’s especially buttery and mild, butterkase pairs well with tangy, acidic foods, like olives, the foods on a relish tray and all kinds of pickles: classic pickles, pickled vegetables and pickled fruit. Their acidity cuts through the richness of the cheese. Butterkase would also be a fantastic addition to a supper club board. Its soft texture is great on crisp crackers studded with nuts and fruits, with a German mustard nearby.

For wine and cheese pairings, opt for something light and refreshing, like Prosecco or an unoaked chardonnay, to balance the richness of the cheese. Even a bottle of inexpensive champagne makes the cheese board feel a little fancier.

Slice butterkase while it’s still cold from the fridge. If it sits for a while, butterkase can become soft enough to spread, making it difficult to slice. As a general rule, Molly and Emilia recommend slicing harder cheeses in advance to get ahead of cheese board prep. Keep backup portions in the fridge to quickly replenish the board as the night goes on.

Aged Gouda pairs well with sweeter fruit jams, chocolate, candied pecans and even tropical fruits like mango. Fruit-and-nut studded crackers work just as well with aged Gouda as they do with butterkase. For dessert, try pairing the cheese with brownies or caramelly stroopwafels. Drink pairings range from red wine to spiced rum.

While there are guidelines for pairing, Emilia encourages people to step out of their comfort zone and explore out-of-the-box options. “There’s no wrong answer to pairing,” she says. “People tend to think that they have to only pair fancy things with cheese, and honestly, some of the best pairings I’ve had have just been snacks or things I love that are lying around the house.” Take a cue from Emilia’s cheese competition days: Try the cheese with whatever you have in the kitchen; you may discover an unexpected favorite. “Get weird with it,” says Emilia.

#6505. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6504. The Coffee Mug I Rave About to Strangers Is on Sale for Black Friday

The Fellow Move Mug is currently on sale for Black Friday. You can now get it for 20% off, bringing the price down to $24 for the 12 oz and $28 for the 16 oz.

I wouldn't call myself a minimalist by any means, but I am not someone who buys a lot of kitchen gadgets or rushes to snag the latest seasonal cup. But ever since I picked up my first Fellow Carter Move Mug five years ago, I’ve happily repurchased it several times.

This sleek little mug, designed by the coffee nerds at Fellow, keeps your brew hot (or cold) without sacrificing flavor. I use it so often that I’ve sung its praises to a coffee shop owner in Washington, a bed-and-breakfast proprietor in Maine, and countless other strangers.

I love this mug more than I can express—so much, in fact, that I reached out to Fellow founder, Jake Miller, to chat about it. He launched the brand 13 years ago with the goal of delivering great design to coffee brewing, but customers kept asking for an exceptional way to drink their coffee on the go. So a company founded by and for coffee obsessives made the ultimate companion container.

The Carter Move Mug is designed with a superior drinking experience in mind. The body of the mug tapers into a thin drinking lip that Miller said was inspired by a wine glass. When you take a sip, you’re touching metal and not paint, and the lip is protected when the mug is closed.

At the time, other to-go cups were designed with a small opening in the lid and completely missed out on the aromatics. “It was a pretty opinionated design choice, but we wanted people to experience the incredible smells of coffee,” he explained. “Once the lid is off, you have this really great drinking experience.” While the lip of the mug is metal, the inside of the mug is ceramic-coated, so it doesn’t impart any taste to the coffee. According to Miller, “that allows for a more pure expression of the coffee.”

When I tell people about the Carter Mug, I like to joke that it’s almost too good at its job. Hot drinks stay very hot for hours, and I regularly find ice in the mug a full day after I first made my chilled version. I once left a mug of hot coffee in a car during a blizzard, and after almost a day, the coffee was still pleasant to drink. Miller said this effective temperature control is from two things: the distance between the two walls and how much vacuum insulation the mug has. Also, Fellow designed the lid to be gasket-tight so there’s minimal heat loss.

One of my favorite features of the Move Mug is the splash guard that clicks into the vessel and prevents big spills while you’re drinking in motion. (As a person prone to mess, this is very helpful.) This element, along with some other accessories, was born out of feedback based on how customers use their mugs, including a straw for cold coffee, a cup holder-friendly size, and the option for a slide top lid. “Everything we do is customer-driven,” Miller noted.

Maybe not important to how your coffee tastes — but important to aesthetics — the Move Mug is sleek and sophisticated, which means it’s suitable for most situations. There’s a nice range of colors, and it looks great in my hand on my commute and on my desk in the office. It’s truly the perfect accessory.

#6503. Is It Safe to Eat from a Charcuterie Board That’s Been Out All Afternoon?

Charcuterie boards are a party favorite, but how long can they safely sit out? Here's what to know before you grab another bite of that wilted cheese.

I totally understand the excitement that comes from spying a gorgeous charcuterie board at a gathering. Between the cheeses, the cured meats and all the little finger foods, there are too many potential combinations to wonder how long everything has been sitting out. But as a registered dietitian, I can’t help thinking about it!

Food safety was a big deal in my studies, and all those lessons about safe cooking temperatures, proper food handling and food storage have stuck with me. After all, cut a few corners here or let food sit out a little too long there, and you could find yourself in a real pickle—one where you risking spoiling all that delicious food you took time to prepare.

So, how long can a charcuterie board safely sit out before it’s time to show it the bin? With the holidays in full swing and cheese boards popping up at just about every gathering, these food safety tips will keep you snacking happily and safely all season long.

Yes, but you’ll want to keep an eye on the clock! Most perishable items on a charcuterie board—including soft cheeses, deli meats, chilled dips and cut fruit—shouldn’t sit at room temperature for more than two hours. If the temperature is above 90°F (like at an outdoor summer party), that window shrinks to just one hour.

Harmful bacteria can multiply quickly when perishable foods spend too much time in the temperature danger zone, which is between 40°F and 140°F. And unfortunately food doesn’t have to look or smell spoiled to be unsafe to eat.

Some charcuterie boards are designed to keep food chilled, with built-in compartments for ice packs or trays that sit over ice. If the perishable foods are kept at 40°F or below, they can stay out a little longer without entering the temperature danger zone.

One thing to keep in mind: The clock starts when the perishable foods come out of the refrigerator, not when guests start digging in. If a charcuterie board has been sitting out for more than two hours, it’s safest to toss the perishable items rather than save them for later.

And if you’re a guest and aren’t sure how long the board has been sitting out, you have a couple options. You can either casually ask the host, or you can skip the perishable items altogether and stick with shelf-stable munchies like crackers, seasoned nuts and pretzels.

Sort of! Hard cheeses like Parmesan, Manchego and aged Gouda handle room temperature better than soft cheeses like Brie, fresh goat cheese, fresh mozzarella and cream cheese.

That’s because hard cheeses contain less moisture, so they’re a little less hospitable to the harmful bacteria that can make you sick. Soft cheeses have more moisture, so they’re more perishable and should follow the same strict two-hour rule as other refrigerated foods.

While hard cheeses are a safer bet than soft varieties, that doesn’t mean they can sit out indefinitely! They’re still subject to food safety concerns, so if you’re not sure how long the board has been sitting out, it’s safest to skip the perishable items regardless of the cheese type.

You can’t always tell if food is safe to eat just by looking at it, but there are a few visible signs that a charcuterie board may have been sitting out for a while. You might notice cheeses sweating or getting extra soft or oily, or you might see sliced meats starting to look dried out around the edges. Cut fruit may also turn mushy or discolored as it sits.

Not everything on a cheese board carries the same food safety risk. When in doubt, don’t take a chance on foods that need refrigeration. You can always fill your plate with the shelf-stable nuts, crackers and whole fruit instead.

If you’re hosting, put out smaller portions of cheeses and meats and replenish the board as needed. That way, you can keep the extra food refrigerated until it’s time to serve more, rather than letting everything sit out for hours.

#6500. These 3-Ingredient Salt Dough Ornaments Are a Christmas Tradition Worth Starting

Some of the most treasured ornaments on my Christmas tree started with a bag of flour.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Of all the ornaments I’ve collected over the years, my two favorites were made in my kitchen about nine Christmases ago. One is my son’s little handprint, cut from a simple salt dough and painted to resemble Santa Claus, with his fingers forming Santa’s white beard. The other is my daughter’s impossibly tiny footprint, turned into a Christmas tree. Neither is a particularly impressive work of art, but I handle them with more care than any of the antique glass ornaments I’ve acquired over the years.

Those two ornaments marked the beginning of what has become an annual Christmas tradition in our house, and our collection of homemade salt dough ornaments has grown quite a bit since. And while the opportunities to capture tiny hands and feet are rather fleeting, the appeal of making our own Christmas ornaments hasn’t diminished much as my children have grown. Our designs have just become more ambitious.

Salt dough is a simple modeling dough made from flour, salt and water. When dried, it hardens into a sturdy material that can be painted, embellished and hung on the tree. When properly dried and stored in a cool, dry place, the ornaments can last for years.

Mix the flour and salt in a bowl, adding the water gradually until you have a soft dough that’s easy to work with. Turn it out onto a floured countertop and knead it for a minute or two until it’s smooth.

I use a chopstick to poke a hole at the top of each ornament for the ribbon. A word of advice from someone who learned this the hard way: Do this before baking. Salt dough is remarkably unforgiving once it’s hardened.

With plain dough, you have the freedom to paint your ornaments to match your Christmas decor, whether that means traditional reds and greens or the colors of your favorite vintage glass baubles.

If you’d like to give your ornaments some extra protection, finish them with a clear craft sealer. Once everything has dried, string them with velvet ribbon, baker’s twine or whatever you have in your craft drawer. Store them somewhere dry after Christmas, and you can add to your collection year after year.

#6499. Breville Oracle Jet Review: This Beginner-Friendly Espresso Machine Is $200 Off Right Now

I’ve had quite a few dreams and aspirations in my adult life thus far. One of them was owning an espresso machine. As someone who would typically choose a cappuccino over a cup of drip coffee, the idea of waking up every morning and enjoying the perfect mug of milky espresso from the comfort of my own home seemed like the pinnacle of luxury.

Besides the obvious barriers to entry of price and counter space, one of the main reasons I waited so long to make my dream a reality was that, well, I was intimidated. The world of coffee—and espresso in particular—is one that intrigues me, but I’m admittedly no expert. And while the science nerd in me feels somewhat compelled to spend time delving deep into grind size and ratios and extraction times, the reality is I’ve always felt daunted at the prospect of actually doing so—and wary of investing in a machine that would be so complicated to use, I’d end up forgoing it anyway. At the same time, I shied away from the idea of fully automatic machines that operate at the push of a button, because the wannabe barista in me wants to feel like I’m doing something as I make my morning cup. That, and I’ve never found the espresso those kinds of machines make to be all that good.

That’s why, when I got wind a couple years ago that Breville was launching a new top of the line, not-quite automatic espresso machine that promised to guide me through all of the processes I was intimidated by, I was immediately intrigued. The machine in question? The Oracle Jet, the latest (at the time of its launch) in Breville’s Oracle line after 2017’s Oracle Touch. The Jet shares many of the same features that made contributor Carina Finn fall in love with the Oracle Touch when she tested it—namely, an easy-to-use touchscreen display with a multitude of drink programs, automatic grinding, dosing, and tamping, and an automatic milk frother. But the newer machine has several key improvements that make it an even better pick for home espresso drinkers—and it's $200 off for Black Friday right now. After years of testing, I can say quite confidently that there is no other machine I’d rather own.

The Oracle Jet is about as close to a super-automatic machine as you can get without actually being super-automatic. That is to say, you still have to complete a few steps along the way to your latte.

After unboxing my machine on its arrival, I was delighted to find that there was no need to flip through a physical manual. The entire setup process was explained (very clearly, I’ll add) via the touchscreen display, and the steps were laid out in a logical order, which I really appreciated.

After the initial set up, the display guided me through making my first drink and calibrating the grind size for the beans I had on hand. I had to make several rounds of espresso to get the ideal grind size (which the machine suggests based on extraction speed). As someone with no espresso machine experience but who likes to know why and how things work, I found this process fun and helpful, a great jumping off point in my own espresso journey.

Within 30 minutes of receiving my machine in the mail, I had set it all up and made a pretty damn good cappuccino—far better than the $6 ones I get from my local coffee shop, that’s for sure. To make a coffee drink, you’ll start by selecting from a catalogue of options (12+ at the time of writing) and inserting the portafilter under the grinder chute. Press the grind icon to begin the grinding process, after which it will automatically be tamped down. Then you’ll move the portafilter over to the group head, twist it into place, and press the brew icon to start the extraction process. The display will count the extraction time for you, and even suggest adjusting the grind size for next time if it notices the extraction taking too long or too short. If you’re making a milk-based drink, the last step is to add your milk of choice to the included stainless steel pitcher, place it under the steam wand, and press the milk frothing icon. The wand will steam the milk to whatever temperature and foam level you’ve selected (and according to which type of milk you used, be it animal or plant-based). After you’ve removed the pitcher, you’ll wipe down the wand and lower it back into place, where it’ll shoot out hot water to purge any remaining milk from the system.

My latte art has come a long way since that first cappuccino!

I won’t bury the lede here: I’m a big fan of this machine. It’s revolutionized my at-home coffee routine, and after owning it for several months, I can’t imagine my life without it at this point. But now you know my stance, I’ll get into some specifics as to what makes this machine so great.

Whether you’re a beginner espresso maker or just tight on time (or both, like me), nothing beats the convenience of a machine that does the hard work of grinding, tamping, and temperature-setting for you. But if the idea of tinkering around with those things is appealing to you, the Oracle Jet offers (some) capability to do so as well. The built-in Baratza burr grinder has 45 grind settings that are easily tweaked by turning a knob on the left side of the machine, or via the touchscreen display, where you can also adjust the temperature at which your drinks are brewed. While there are some 12+ preset programs for drinks ranging from flat whites to cold brew (more on that later), you can also customize your own drink settings and save them to the system.

Everything about the Oracle Jet feels well thought out and intuitive. I’m not just talking about the actual brewing process here, either: There are a number of little design choices that go a long way in making the user experience more enjoyable, like a lever at the base of the machine that lets you lock it in place or unlock wheels if you need to move it around. I also appreciate that there’s a way to fill the water tank from the front of the machine, without needing to remove the whole tank.

One common complaint with espresso machines is that they can take a long time to heat up. Our top espresso machine pick, for instance, takes at least 20 minutes to stabilize the temperature in its boilers. Not so with the Oracle Jet, which can start brewing espresso pretty much immediately after you turn it on. The reason for this is that it uses Breville’s ThermoJet heating system rather than a traditional boiler heating system found in many high-end espresso machines (including the others in the Oracle line). While this means you can’t brew and steam at the same time, you can quickly switch between the two (read: you can start steaming milk immediately after your espresso is extracted). As someone who is often making her coffee in a haphazard rush to get out the door in the morning, that immediacy is crucial for me. This difference in heating systems is also one of the reasons the Oracle Jet is $800 less expensive than the Oracle Touch, which uses a traditional dual boiler.

The advanced touchscreen display on the Oracle Jet is so responsive and smooth that using it almost feels like using a smartphone. And unlike the Oracle Touch, the Jet can connect to WiFi and, therefore, get firmware updates as they become available.

I love that the Oracle Jet has programs for brewing “cold brew” and “cold espresso,” but that “cold brew” is more so an approximation of the stuff than actual cold brewed coffee. It’s made with a three-minute extraction at a lower temperature, and while I found the resulting coffee enjoyable to drink, this will never quite compare to a cup of cold brew made using a several hours-long extraction process.

In short, not much. But there are a few nitpicky qualms I’ve discovered over the course of several months using the machine. One is that the spouts on the portafilter and the hot water spout on the machine are set fairly far apart, which means there have been times when I’ve gone to make an Americano and the hot water has entirely missed my mug. This can, of course, be remedied by using a wider mug or adjusting its position after the espresso is brewed. I also wish there was some kind of sensor that could safeguard against accidentally starting the brewing process when I’ve forgotten to move the portafilter over from the grinder to the group head—though I will say, stopping the process when I’ve made mistakes like this is as easy as tapping the brew icon again.

There is, of course, the matter of price. At $2,000, this is an expensive machine—there’s no getting around that. It is also relatively large, but I will note that it fits quite comfortably on the sliver of counter space between the fridge and the sink in my kitchen. And that $2000 price tag is within the realm of expected for good automatic coffee machines with features like the Oracle Jet.

Look, I’m not going to tell anyone they need a $2,000 espresso machine. But if you find yourself buying milk-based espresso drinks on a near-daily basis and want a machine that makes the process of brewing them yourself fun and easy, I think it’s well worth considering, especially given that it's currently on sale for $200 off. It’s certainly earned my stamp of approval. If you do buy it, chances are you’ll soon be making drinks that are markedly better than the ones you’re spending upwards of $6 on at your local coffee shop—and if you do the math, the machine will practically pay for itself in less than a year.

If you’re in the market for a cheaper, no-frills (but still very beginner-friendly) machine, you may want to check out our review of the Breville Bambino Plus instead. Or head to our full review of the best espresso machines for even more options, all vetted by our team of product testers.

The first time writer Ali Domrongchai went to Thailand with her grandmother, they had a mission: eat as many khanom (the Thai word for desserts and small snacks) as possible. They wandered from market to market, weaving through the stalls and sharing everything that caught their eye. Their hands-down favorite was the khanom tom, which her grandmother grew up buying from a street vendor in Bangkok as an after-school treat. Traditionally made with both fresh coconut and coconut milk, the bite-size sweets are chewy, fragrant, and irresistible.

After a quick boil, each ball is rolled in shredded fresh coconut for a soft, snowy finish.
